<!-- Source: https://seonwkim.github.io/actor-spring-boot-starter/guides/core/behaviors/ -->

# Behaviors

An actor's behavior says how it handles each message. You build it in `create` with
`SpringActorBehavior.builder(...)` (or `behavior<C>(...) { }` in Kotlin, see the
[Kotlin guide](../kotlin.md#defining-an-actor)). This page covers what you can
do inside a behavior: keep state, choose the next behavior, react to lifecycle signals, schedule
messages with timers, watch other actors, and turn futures into messages.

For defining and spawning actors see [Actors](actors.md); for sending messages see
[Messaging](messaging.md).

## The builder

| Builder method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `withState(ctx -> state)` | Creates the actor's state object when the actor starts (and again on each restart). Handlers then receive the state instead of the context. |
| `onMessage(Type.class, (state, msg) -> next)` | Handles messages of `Type`. Handlers are tried in the order they were added; the first whose type matches runs. |
| `onSignal(Signal.class, (state, signal) -> next)` | Handles a lifecycle signal: `PreRestart`, `PostStop` or `ActorTerminated`. |
| `withSupervisionStrategy(strategy)` | What happens when a handler throws. See [Supervision](supervision.md). |
| `withMdc(msg -> map)` | Log context computed per message. See [Logging](logging.md). |
| `build()` | Returns the behavior. |

A message with no matching handler is *unhandled*: it is dropped (and published as unhandled), and the
actor keeps going.

## State with withState

Without `withState`, every handler receives the behavior context (`ctx`). With it, the handlers receive
your own state object, which you usually give a reference to the context. Put the actor's fields and its
handler methods in that object:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Component
    public class CounterActor implements SpringActor<CounterActor.Command> {

        public interface Command {}

        public record Add(long amount) implements Command {}

        public static class Get extends AskCommand<Long> implements Command {}

        @Override
        public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
            return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                    .withState(ctx -> new Counter(ctx, actorContext.actorId()))
                    .onMessage(Add.class, Counter::onAdd)
                    .onMessage(Get.class, Counter::onGet)
                    .build();
        }

        private static class Counter {
            private final SpringBehaviorContext<Command> ctx;
            private final String id;
            private long value;   // only this actor's thread touches it

            Counter(SpringBehaviorContext<Command> ctx, String id) {
                this.ctx = ctx;
                this.id = id;
                ctx.getLog().info("Counter {} started", id);
            }

            SpringActorBehavior<Command> onAdd(Add msg) {
                value += msg.amount();
                return SpringActorBehavior.same();
            }

            SpringActorBehavior<Command> onGet(Get msg) {
                msg.reply(value);
                return SpringActorBehavior.same();
            }
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @Component
    class CounterActor : SpringActor<CounterActor.Command> {

        sealed interface Command

        data class Add(val amount: Long) : Command

        class Get : AskCommand<Long>(), Command

        override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
            behavior<Command, Counter>(actorContext, state = { ctx -> Counter(ctx, actorContext.actorId()) }) {
                // The handlers run with the Counter as `this`.
                onMessage<Add> { msg -> onAdd(msg) }
                onMessage<Get> { msg -> onGet(msg) }
            }

        private class Counter(private val ctx: SpringBehaviorContext<Command>, private val id: String) {
            private var value = 0L   // only this actor's thread touches it

            init {
                ctx.log.info("Counter {} started", id)
            }

            fun onAdd(msg: Add): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
                value += msg.amount
                return SpringActorBehavior.same()
            }

            fun onGet(msg: Get): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
                msg.reply(value)
                return SpringActorBehavior.same()
            }
        }
    }
    ```

The state object belongs to one actor and is only touched while that actor handles a message, so plain
fields need no `volatile` or locks. Don't hand the object (or its mutable collections) to other threads.

The `withState` factory runs inside the actor when it starts, before the first message. It is the place
to load initial data, start timers, register with the [receptionist](receptionist.md) or spawn children.
On a [restart](supervision.md#what-a-restart-keeps-and-what-it-loses) it runs again and builds a fresh
object.

## What a handler returns

Each handler returns the behavior for the next message:

| Return | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `SpringActorBehavior.same()` | Keep handling messages the same way. The usual return. |
| `SpringActorBehavior.stopped()` | Stop the actor after this message. Its `PostStop` handler runs. |
| `SpringActorBehavior.unhandled()` | This handler didn't handle the message after all. The message is published as unhandled; the behavior stays. |
| A new behavior from `SpringActorBehavior.builder(...).build()` | Handle the next messages with this behavior instead. |

Returning a new behavior lets an actor change how it reacts, for example a door that ignores `Open` while
locked. Each built behavior has its own handlers and its own state:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Component
    public class DoorActor implements SpringActor<DoorActor.Command> {

        public interface Command {}
        public record Lock() implements Command {}
        public record Unlock() implements Command {}
        public static class IsLocked extends AskCommand<Boolean> implements Command {}

        @Override
        public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
            return unlocked(actorContext);
        }

        private static SpringActorBehavior<Command> unlocked(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
            return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                    .onMessage(Lock.class, (ctx, msg) -> locked(actorContext))
                    .onMessage(IsLocked.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                        msg.reply(false);
                        return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                    })
                    .build();
        }

        private static SpringActorBehavior<Command> locked(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
            return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                    .onMessage(Unlock.class, (ctx, msg) -> unlocked(actorContext))
                    .onMessage(IsLocked.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                        msg.reply(true);
                        return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                    })
                    .build();
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @Component
    class DoorActor : SpringActor<DoorActor.Command> {

        sealed interface Command
        class Lock : Command
        class Unlock : Command
        class IsLocked : AskCommand<Boolean>(), Command

        override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
            unlocked(actorContext)

        private fun unlocked(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
            behavior<Command>(actorContext) {
                onMessage<Lock> { locked(actorContext) }
                onMessage<IsLocked> { msg ->
                    msg.reply(false)
                    same()
                }
            }

        private fun locked(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
            behavior<Command>(actorContext) {
                onMessage<Unlock> { unlocked(actorContext) }
                onMessage<IsLocked> { msg ->
                    msg.reply(true)
                    same()
                }
            }
    }
    ```

In the locked behavior, `Lock` has no handler, so a second `Lock` is unhandled and dropped. For many
actors a status field in one state object is simpler; switch behaviors when the states really accept
different messages.

## Lifecycle signals

Signals are events about the actor's life, not messages from others. Handle them with `onSignal`:

| Signal | When it arrives | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `PreRestart` | Just before a supervised restart | Release resources the old state holds; log what is lost |
| `PostStop` | After the actor stopped (for any reason) | Close resources, deregister, log final state |
| `ActorTerminated` | An actor this one [watches](#watching-other-actors) has stopped; `signal.ref()` is that actor | Replace a worker, clean up a session |

An example with `PreRestart` and `PostStop` is in [Supervision](supervision.md#reacting-to-restarts-and-stops).
A signal handler returns the next behavior like a message handler; return `same()`.

## Timers

A timer sends a message to the actor itself, once or repeatedly. Use timers for timeouts, retries,
polling and periodic work. Each timer has a key (any object); starting a timer with a key that is
already active replaces it.

| Method on the context | What it does |
|---|---|
| `startSingleTimer(key, message, delay)` | Sends `message` once after `delay` |
| `startTimerAtFixedRate(key, message, interval)` | Sends `message` every `interval` until cancelled |
| `cancelTimer(key)` | Cancels the timer; a message it already sent is not delivered |

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Component
    public class SessionActor implements SpringActor<SessionActor.Command> {

        public interface Command {}
        public record Touch() implements Command {}
        private enum IdleTimeout implements Command { INSTANCE }
        private enum Flush implements Command { INSTANCE }

        private static final Duration IDLE = Duration.ofMinutes(30);

        @Override
        public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
            return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                    .withState(ctx -> {
                        ctx.startTimerAtFixedRate("flush", Flush.INSTANCE, Duration.ofSeconds(10));
                        ctx.startSingleTimer("idle", IdleTimeout.INSTANCE, IDLE);
                        return ctx;
                    })
                    .onMessage(Touch.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                        ctx.startSingleTimer("idle", IdleTimeout.INSTANCE, IDLE);   // restart the idle clock
                        return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                    })
                    .onMessage(Flush.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                        ctx.getLog().debug("Flushing");
                        return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                    })
                    .onMessage(IdleTimeout.class, (ctx, msg) -> SpringActorBehavior.stopped())
                    .build();
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @Component
    class SessionActor : SpringActor<SessionActor.Command> {

        sealed interface Command
        class Touch : Command
        private data object IdleTimeout : Command
        private data object Flush : Command

        override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
            behavior<Command, _>(actorContext, state = { ctx ->
                ctx.startTimerAtFixedRate("flush", Flush, 10.seconds)
                ctx.startSingleTimer("idle", IdleTimeout, IDLE)
                ctx
            }) {
                onMessage<Touch> {
                    startSingleTimer("idle", IdleTimeout, IDLE)   // restart the idle clock
                    same()
                }
                onMessage<Flush> {
                    log.debug("Flushing")
                    same()
                }
                onMessage<IdleTimeout> { stopped() }
            }

        private companion object {
            val IDLE = 30.minutes
        }
    }
    ```

Timers belong to the actor: they stop when it stops and are cancelled when it restarts. Timer messages
go through the mailbox like any other message, so they run one at a time with the rest.

## Watching other actors

`ctx.watch(ref)` asks to be told when another actor stops. When it does, this actor receives the
`ActorTerminated` signal with the stopped actor's ref:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    .onMessage(Track.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
        ctx.watch(msg.worker());
        return SpringActorBehavior.same();
    })
    .onSignal(ActorTerminated.class, (ctx, signal) -> {
        ctx.getLog().info("{} stopped", signal.ref().path());
        return SpringActorBehavior.same();
    })
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    onMessage<Track> { msg ->
        watch(msg.worker)
        same()
    }
    onSignal<ActorTerminated> { signal ->
        log.info("{} stopped", signal.ref.path())
        same()
    }
    ```

!!! warning "Always handle ActorTerminated when you watch"
    An actor that watches another and has no `onSignal(ActorTerminated.class, ...)` handler **fails**
    when the watched actor stops, and its supervision strategy applies (stop, by default).

The watched actor can be anywhere: a child, an unrelated actor, or (in cluster mode) an actor on another
node; it then also counts as stopped when its node leaves the cluster. The chat example's `UserActor`
watches the actor that represents the WebSocket client so it can clean up when the client goes away.

## Futures: pipeToSelf

Handlers must not block, and callbacks on a `CompletionStage` run on another thread, where they must not
touch the actor's state. `ctx.pipeToSelf(stage, (value, error) -> message)` solves both: when the stage
completes, the function builds a message, and the actor handles it like any other.

=== "Java"

    ```java
    .onMessage(Load.class, (state, msg) -> {
        state.ctx().pipeToSelf(
                profileClient.fetch(msg.userId()),        // CompletionStage<Profile>
                (profile, error) -> new Loaded(profile, error));
        return SpringActorBehavior.same();
    })
    .onMessage(Loaded.class, (state, msg) -> state.onLoaded(msg))   // update state here
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    onMessage<Load> { msg ->
        ctx.pipeToSelf(profileClient.fetch(msg.userId)) { profile, error ->   // CompletionStage<Profile>
            Loaded(profile, error)
        }
        same()
    }
    onMessage<Loaded> { msg -> onLoaded(msg) }   // update state here
    ```

Exactly one of `value` and `error` is non-null. More examples, including asking another actor, are in
[Messaging](messaging.md#asking-from-inside-an-actor).

## The behavior context

The context (`SpringBehaviorContext<C>`) is what an actor can do from its handlers. You get it in the
`withState` factory, and as the first handler argument when there is no `withState` (in the Kotlin
`behavior { }` DSL, as the handler's `this`).

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `getSelf()` | A handle to this actor: pass it as a reply address, or use it for [child operations](actors.md#child-actors) |
| `getLog()` | The actor's logger; its lines carry the actor's path and MDC (see [Logging](logging.md)) |
| `actorId()` | The id the actor was spawned with, so handlers don't have to capture it in `create` |
| `path()`, `nodeAddress()` | The actor's path and the address of the node it runs on |
| `getChild(ChildClass.class, id)`, `getChildren()` | The running child with that class and id (an `Optional`), and all running children. `getChild(name)`, which took the internal name `<ClassName>:<id>`, is deprecated |
| `stop(child)` | Stops one of this actor's children |
| `startSingleTimer`, `startTimerAtFixedRate`, `cancelTimer` | [Timers](#timers) |
| `watch(ref)` | [Watching](#watching-other-actors) |
| `pipeToSelf(stage, fn)` | [Futures](#futures-pipetoself) |
| `messageAdapter(Type.class, fn)` | A ref that accepts another actor's reply type and delivers it as one of this actor's commands. See [Messaging](messaging.md#replying-to-an-actor-without-ask). |
| `registerWithReceptionist(name)` | Registers this actor under a service name. See [Receptionist](receptionist.md). |
| `unwrap(Class)` | The underlying Pekko `ActorContext`, for features the starter doesn't wrap |

Use the context only on the actor's own thread: inside handlers and the `withState` factory, never in a
future callback.

## Stashing and other Pekko features

The starter has no stash (holding messages back until the actor is ready). The usual replacement is a
queue in the state object, as the `AgentBrain` of the [agent example](../../examples/agent.md) does: while
it is busy it adds new `Chat` messages to a `Deque` and takes the next one when the turn ends.

For a Pekko feature the starter doesn't wrap, there are two escape hatches. Code that uses them depends
on Pekko directly and gets no compatibility promise from the starter.

- `ctx.unwrap(org.apache.pekko.actor.typed.javadsl.ActorContext.class)` returns Pekko's context.
- `SpringActorBehavior.wrap(pekkoBehavior)` runs a behavior written against Pekko's API. Such a behavior
  gets none of the starter's features (child operations, MDC, metrics hooks).

## Pitfalls

- **Blocking in a handler.** Use `pipeToSelf` for futures, and the blocking dispatcher for blocking I/O.
- **Touching state from a callback.** `thenAccept` on a future runs on another thread. Send a message
  with `pipeToSelf` instead.
- **Watching without handling `ActorTerminated`.** The watcher fails when the watched actor stops.
- **Heavy work in `withState`.** The actor handles no message until the factory returns. Load large data asynchronously with `pipeToSelf`.
- **Handler order.** The first handler whose type matches wins. Register specific types before their
  supertypes.

## Related

- [Actors](actors.md): defining, spawning and stopping actors
- [Messaging](messaging.md): tell, ask and message adapters
- [Supervision](supervision.md): restarts and what they reset
- [Logging](logging.md): per-message MDC with `withMdc`
- [Testing](../testing.md): testing behaviors

<!-- Source: https://seonwkim.github.io/actor-spring-boot-starter/guides/core/routers/ -->

# Routers

A router is an actor that owns a pool of identical worker actors and passes each message it receives to
one of them (or to all of them). You send to the router as if it were one actor; the work runs on several
workers at once.

Use a router when one actor can't keep up and the work doesn't depend on shared state: sending emails,
resizing images, calling a slow API. If the work belongs to an entity (an order, a user), use one actor
per entity instead (see [Actors](actors.md) or [Sharded actors](../cluster/sharded-actors.md)); a router
with [consistent hashing](#consistent-hashing) sits in between.

A router lives on one node, and its workers are its children. Routers come with the core starter; no
extra dependency or configuration is needed.

## Creating a router

A router has two parts: the worker actor that does the work, and the router actor that holds the pool.
They share one command type.

=== "Java"

    ```java
    // The worker: an ordinary actor bean
    @Component
    public class ResizeWorker implements SpringActor<ImageRouter.Command> {

        private final ImageService imageService;

        public ResizeWorker(ImageService imageService) {
            this.imageService = imageService;
        }

        @Override
        public SpringActorBehavior<ImageRouter.Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
            return SpringActorBehavior.builder(ImageRouter.Command.class, actorContext)
                    .onMessage(ImageRouter.Resize.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                        imageService.resize(msg.imageId(), msg.width());
                        return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                    })
                    .build();
        }
    }

    // The router: its behavior is a pool of ResizeWorkers
    @Component
    public class ImageRouter implements SpringActor<ImageRouter.Command> {

        public interface Command {}

        public record Resize(String imageId, int width) implements Command {}

        @Override
        public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
            return SpringRouterBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                    .withRoutingStrategy(RoutingStrategy.roundRobin())
                    .withPoolSize(8)
                    .withWorkerActors(ResizeWorker.class)
                    .withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart())
                    .build();
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    // The worker: an ordinary actor bean
    @Component
    class ResizeWorker(private val imageService: ImageService) : SpringActor<ImageRouter.Command> {

        override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<ImageRouter.Command> =
            actorBehavior<ImageRouter.Command>(actorContext)
                .onMessage(ImageRouter.Resize::class.java) { _, msg ->
                    imageService.resize(msg.imageId, msg.width)
                    SpringActorBehavior.same()
                }
                .build()
    }

    // The router: its behavior is a pool of ResizeWorkers
    @Component
    class ImageRouter : SpringActor<ImageRouter.Command> {

        sealed interface Command

        data class Resize(val imageId: String, val width: Int) : Command

        override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
            SpringRouterBehavior.builder(Command::class.java, actorContext)
                .withRoutingStrategy(RoutingStrategy.roundRobin())
                .withPoolSize(8)
                .withWorkerActors(ResizeWorker::class.java)
                .withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart())
                .build()
    }
    ```

Spawn and use the router like any other actor:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Service
    public class ImageResizer {
        private final SpringActorSystem actorSystem;

        public ImageResizer(SpringActorSystem actorSystem) {
            this.actorSystem = actorSystem;
        }

        public void resizeLater(String imageId) {
            actorSystem.getOrSpawn(ImageRouter.class, "image-router")
                    .thenAccept(router -> router.tell(new ImageRouter.Resize(imageId, 640)));
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @Service
    class ImageResizer(private val actorSystem: SpringActorSystem) {

        suspend fun resizeLater(imageId: String) {
            actorSystem.awaitGetOrSpawn<ImageRouter, _>("image-router")
                .tell(ImageRouter.Resize(imageId, 640))
        }
    }
    ```

## Builder options

| Method | Required | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `withRoutingStrategy(strategy)` | yes | none | `build()` throws `IllegalStateException` without it |
| `withWorkerActors(Class)` | yes | none | A `SpringActor` bean whose command type is the router's |
| `withPoolSize(n)` | no | 5 | Must be positive |
| `withSupervisionStrategy(strategy)` | no | stop | Applies to each worker. See [Worker failures](#worker-failures). |

Each worker's `create(actorContext)` gets its own id, `worker-<uuid>` (`actorContext.actorId()`), which it
keeps across restarts. Use it to tell workers apart in logs.

## Routing strategies

| Strategy | Who gets a message | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `RoutingStrategy.roundRobin()` | Each worker in turn | Tasks that take about the same time |
| `RoutingStrategy.random()` | A random worker | Simple spreading with no bookkeeping |
| `RoutingStrategy.broadcast()` | Every worker | Telling all workers something, such as "clear your cache" |
| `RoutingStrategy.consistentHashing()` | The worker chosen by the message's key | Keeping all messages for one key on one worker |

### Broadcast

With `broadcast()`, every message is handled once per worker: 10 messages to a pool of 5 means 50
handler calls. Use it for rare control messages, not for regular work. A broadcast ask gets the first
worker's reply; the other replies are dropped.

### Consistent hashing

`consistentHashing()` sends messages with the same key to the same worker, as long as the pool doesn't
change. A worker can then keep a cache per key, or handle one customer's messages in order. Give a
message its key by implementing `ConsistentHashable`:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    public record ProcessOrder(String customerId, String orderId) implements Command, ConsistentHashable {
        @Override
        public String getConsistentHashKey() {
            return customerId;   // one customer's orders always go to the same worker
        }
    }

    // In the router's create():
    return SpringRouterBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
            .withRoutingStrategy(RoutingStrategy.consistentHashing())
            .withPoolSize(10)
            .withWorkerActors(OrderWorker.class)
            .build();
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    data class ProcessOrder(val customerId: String, val orderId: String) : Command, ConsistentHashable {
        // one customer's orders always go to the same worker
        override fun getConsistentHashKey(): String = customerId
    }

    // In the router's create():
    SpringRouterBehavior.builder(Command::class.java, actorContext)
        .withRoutingStrategy(RoutingStrategy.consistentHashing())
        .withPoolSize(10)
        .withWorkerActors(OrderWorker::class.java)
        .build()
    ```

- The key must not be `null`; a `null` key fails the routing with `IllegalStateException`.
- A message that doesn't implement `ConsistentHashable` is hashed by its `toString()`. Records and data
  classes have a stable `toString()`; most other classes don't, so implement `ConsistentHashable`.
- `consistentHashing(virtualNodesFactor)` sets how many points each worker gets on the hash ring
  (default 10, minimum 1). More points spread keys more evenly.
- This is not a replacement for sharding: the mapping changes when a worker is replaced, and it stays on
  one node. For one actor per key across a cluster, use [sharded actors](../cluster/sharded-actors.md).

## Ask through a router

A router forwards `AskCommand`s like any message, and the worker that handles it replies to the asker:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    public static class Validate extends AskCommand<Boolean> implements Command {
        public final String data;

        public Validate(String data) {
            this.data = data;
        }
    }

    // In the worker:
    .onMessage(Validate.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
        msg.reply(!msg.data.isBlank());
        return SpringActorBehavior.same();
    })

    // The caller:
    CompletionStage<Boolean> valid = router.ask(new ValidationRouter.Validate("payload"))
            .withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
            .execute();
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    class Validate(val data: String) : AskCommand<Boolean>(), Command

    // In the worker:
    .onMessage(Validate::class.java) { _, msg ->
        msg.reply(msg.data.isNotBlank())
        SpringActorBehavior.same()
    }

    // The caller, in a suspend function:
    val valid: Boolean = router.awaitAsk(ValidationRouter.Validate("payload"), timeout = 2.seconds)
    ```

## Worker failures

The router's `withSupervisionStrategy` applies to each worker. Without it, a worker whose handler throws
**stops** and leaves the pool, so the pool shrinks with every failure. For a pool that should keep its
size, set `SupervisionStrategy.restart()` (or `restart().withLimit(...)`). With restart, the failed
message is dropped and the other messages are still handled, as the router tests check. See
[Supervision](supervision.md) for what each strategy does.

## Workers and Spring beans

Every worker in a pool is created from the same worker bean, so:

- Injected services are shared by all workers (and by every pool that uses the bean). That is what you
  want for repositories, clients and connection pools.
- Per-worker state belongs in the worker's [`withState`](behaviors.md#state-with-withstate) object, not
  in a field of the bean.
- Workers don't have ids of their own. All workers of a pool get the same generated
  `actorContext.actorId()` (`worker-<uuid>`), so don't use it to tell workers apart.

A worker that blocks (JDBC, blocking HTTP) holds a thread of the router's dispatcher. Spawn the router
with `withBlockingDispatcher()` or a [custom dispatcher](dispatchers.md) in that case.

## Pitfalls

- **No routing strategy.** `build()` fails; there is no default strategy.
- **Pool that shrinks.** Without a restart strategy, failing workers stop for good.
- **Shared state in the worker bean.** All workers of all pools share it.
- **Ordering.** Round robin and random spread consecutive messages over different workers, so they can be
  handled out of order. Use consistent hashing (or one actor per key) when order per key matters.

## Related

- [Actors](actors.md): spawning the router
- [Supervision](supervision.md): worker strategies
- [Dispatchers](dispatchers.md): thread pools for blocking workers
- [Sharded actors](../cluster/sharded-actors.md): one actor per key across a cluster
- [Pekko routers](https://pekko.apache.org/docs/pekko/current/typed/routers.html): the pool router the starter uses

<!-- Source: https://seonwkim.github.io/actor-spring-boot-starter/guides/core/pub-sub-topics/ -->

# Pub/Sub Topics

A topic delivers each published message to every actor subscribed to it. The publisher doesn't know who
the subscribers are or how many there are. In cluster mode, a message published on one node reaches the
subscribers on every node.

Use a topic for one-to-many messages: chat rooms, live notifications, "this data changed" events that
several actors care about. Don't use it for:

- one-to-one messages: send to the actor directly ([Messaging](messaging.md));
- request and reply: use ask;
- messages that must not be lost: topics deliver at most once;
- spreading work so that only one worker handles each message: use a [router](routers.md).

Topics come with the core starter. The `SpringTopicManager` bean is created for you.

## Names and message types

A topic is identified by a `TopicName`: a message type plus a name. Publishers and subscribers that use
the same type and name share the topic, on every node. Two topics with the same name but different
types are different topics.

The type matters because **subscribers receive the messages as commands**. A topic's type must be the
subscribers' command type (or a supertype of it): an actor of `SpringActor<UserActor.Command>` can
subscribe to a topic of `UserActor.Command`, and every message published there must be a
`UserActor.Command`.

=== "Java"

    ```java
    // In UserActor: the events users receive are some of its commands
    public interface Command extends JsonSerializable {}
    public record ChatPosted(String roomId, String userId, String text) implements Command {}

    // The topic for one room
    TopicName<UserActor.Command> room = TopicName.of(UserActor.Command.class, "chat-room-" + roomId);
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    // In UserActor: the events users receive are some of its commands
    sealed interface Command : JsonSerializable
    data class ChatPosted(val roomId: String, val userId: String, val text: String) : Command

    // The topic for one room
    val room: TopicName<UserActor.Command> = TopicName.of(UserActor.Command::class.java, "chat-room-$roomId")
    ```

In cluster mode, messages cross nodes, so the message type must implement `JsonSerializable` or
`CborSerializable`. In local mode they don't have to.

## Getting a topic

Inject `SpringTopicManager` and call `topic(name)`, then one of:

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `getOrCreate()` | Returns the topic, creating it on this node if it doesn't exist yet. Safe to call any number of times. |
| `create()` | Creates the topic; throws `TopicAlreadyExistsException` if it already exists on this node |
| `getOrCreateAsync()`, `createAsync()` | The same without blocking: a `CompletionStage` that completes with the topic or fails with the same exception |
| `withTimeout(duration)` | How long they may wait (default 5 s). On timeout they fail with `TopicCreationTimeoutException`. |

`getOrCreate()` and `create()` **block the calling thread** until the topic is ready (usually much less
than a millisecond). That is fine in a service, but not on an actor's thread: there, use the async form and
receive the topic as a message with `pipeToSelf`, as the [chat example](../../examples/chat.md)'s room
actor does. Call them once and keep the `SpringTopicRef`, for example in a service field or in an actor's
state:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Service
    public class AnnouncementService {
        private final SpringTopicRef<UserActor.Command> announcements;

        public AnnouncementService(SpringTopicManager topics) {
            this.announcements = topics
                    .topic(TopicName.of(UserActor.Command.class, "announcements"))
                    .getOrCreate();
        }

        public void announce(String text) {
            announcements.publish(new UserActor.ChatPosted("all", "system", text));
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @Service
    class AnnouncementService(topics: SpringTopicManager) {

        private val announcements: SpringTopicRef<UserActor.Command> = topics
            .topic(TopicName.of(UserActor.Command::class.java, "announcements"))
            .getOrCreate()

        fun announce(text: String) {
            announcements.publish(UserActor.ChatPosted("all", "system", text))
        }
    }
    ```

## Publishing and subscribing

| Method on `SpringTopicRef<T>` | What it does |
|---|---|
| `publish(message)` | Sends the message to every current subscriber. Returns at once. With no subscribers, the message is dropped. |
| `subscribe(ref)` | Delivers the topic's messages to `ref` until it unsubscribes or stops. Subscribing twice is the same as once. |
| `unsubscribe(ref)` | Stops delivery to `ref`. Unsubscribing an actor that isn't subscribed does nothing. |
| `name()` | The topic's `TopicName` |
| `unwrap(Class)` | Pekko's topic actor, for features the starter doesn't wrap |

`subscribe` and `unsubscribe` take any `SpringActorRef`: a handle from `getOrSpawn`, `ctx.getSelf()`, or a
ref received in a message. A subscriber that stops is removed from the topic for you.

Subscribing takes effect shortly after the call, not instantly. A message published right after
`subscribe` can miss the new subscriber. In cluster mode, it also takes a moment for other nodes to learn
about a new subscriber.

## Example: chat rooms

The [chat example](../../examples/chat.md) has one actor per room and one per connected user. The room
actor owns the room's topic: it subscribes users when they join and publishes what they say. Simplified
from its `ChatRoomActor`:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Component
    public class ChatRoomActor implements SpringActor<ChatRoomActor.Command> {

        private final SpringTopicManager topics;

        public ChatRoomActor(SpringTopicManager topics) {
            this.topics = topics;
        }

        public interface Command extends JsonSerializable {}

        public record JoinRoom(String userId, SpringActorRef<UserActor.Command> user) implements Command {}
        public record LeaveRoom(String userId, SpringActorRef<UserActor.Command> user) implements Command {}
        public record SendMessage(String userId, String text) implements Command {}

        @Override
        public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
            String roomId = actorContext.actorId();
            SpringTopicRef<UserActor.Command> roomTopic = topics
                    .topic(TopicName.of(UserActor.Command.class, "chat-room-" + roomId))
                    .getOrCreate();

            return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                    .onMessage(JoinRoom.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                        roomTopic.subscribe(msg.user());
                        return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                    })
                    .onMessage(LeaveRoom.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                        roomTopic.unsubscribe(msg.user());
                        return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                    })
                    .onMessage(SendMessage.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                        roomTopic.publish(new UserActor.ChatPosted(roomId, msg.userId(), msg.text()));
                        return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                    })
                    .build();
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @Component
    class ChatRoomActor(private val topics: SpringTopicManager) : SpringActor<ChatRoomActor.Command> {

        sealed interface Command : JsonSerializable

        data class JoinRoom(val userId: String, val user: SpringActorRef<UserActor.Command>) : Command
        data class LeaveRoom(val userId: String, val user: SpringActorRef<UserActor.Command>) : Command
        data class SendMessage(val userId: String, val text: String) : Command

        override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
            val roomId = actorContext.actorId()
            val roomTopic: SpringTopicRef<UserActor.Command> = topics
                .topic(TopicName.of(UserActor.Command::class.java, "chat-room-$roomId"))
                .getOrCreate()

            return actorBehavior<Command>(actorContext)
                .onMessage(JoinRoom::class.java) { _, msg ->
                    roomTopic.subscribe(msg.user)
                    SpringActorBehavior.same()
                }
                .onMessage(LeaveRoom::class.java) { _, msg ->
                    roomTopic.unsubscribe(msg.user)
                    SpringActorBehavior.same()
                }
                .onMessage(SendMessage::class.java) { _, msg ->
                    roomTopic.publish(UserActor.ChatPosted(roomId, msg.userId, msg.text))
                    SpringActorBehavior.same()
                }
                .build()
        }
    }
    ```

This simplified version blocks the actor's thread in `create()` until the topic exists. The example's
real room actor is a [sharded actor](../cluster/sharded-actors.md), so each room lives on one node of the
cluster while its users can be on any node, and it gets the topic with `getOrCreateAsync()` and
`pipeToSelf` instead of blocking.

## Delivery guarantees

- **At most once.** A message reaches each subscriber once or not at all. Messages to a subscriber that
  is stopping, on a node that is unreachable, or that subscribed a moment too late are lost.
- **Order.** Messages from one publisher arrive at each subscriber in the order they were published.
- **No history.** A new subscriber gets only messages published after it joined. To show recent history,
  keep it in an actor or a database and send it when someone joins.

## Pitfalls

- **Topic type and subscriber type differ.** `subscribe` takes a `SpringActorRef<T>` of the topic's
  type, so the compiler stops a mismatch. Make published events part of the subscribers' command type.
- **Creating topics on every call.** `getOrCreate()` blocks the caller briefly. Keep the ref.
- **Blocking an actor's thread.** Inside an actor, use `getOrCreateAsync()` with `pipeToSelf`.
- **Using `create()` where `getOrCreate()` is meant.** `create()` throws if the topic already exists.
- **Expecting delivery.** For messages that must arrive, send them directly and confirm with ask, or
  store them first.

## Related

- [Messaging](messaging.md): direct messages and ask
- [Receptionist](receptionist.md): finding actors by service name
- [Routers](routers.md): one message to one of many workers
- [Chat example](../../examples/chat.md): topics with sharded rooms
- [Cluster formation](../cluster/cluster-formation.md): running topics across nodes

<!-- Source: https://seonwkim.github.io/actor-spring-boot-starter/guides/core/receptionist/ -->

# Receptionist (Service Discovery)

The receptionist finds actors by a **service name** instead of by class and id. Actors register under a
name; other code looks the name up once, or subscribes and is told whenever the set of registered actors
changes. In cluster mode, the registrations are shared across nodes, so a lookup on one node finds
actors on every node. It wraps Pekko's typed
[Receptionist](https://pekko.apache.org/docs/pekko/current/typed/actor-discovery.html).

Use it when the caller doesn't know (or shouldn't know) the ids of the actors it needs:

- finding all instances of a worker, wherever they run;
- reacting when instances of a service start and stop;
- reaching actors on other cluster nodes without sharding them.

When you know the id, use `getOrSpawn` or `get` ([Actors](actors.md)) or a
[sharded actor](../cluster/sharded-actors.md) instead. To send one message to many actors, a
[topic](pub-sub-topics.md) is simpler.

The `SpringReceptionist` bean comes with the core starter. It is created with
`@ConditionalOnMissingBean`, so you can replace it with your own bean.

## Service names

A `ServiceName` combines a message type and an id. Names with the same type and id are equal on every
node. The type is the command type of the registered actors, so lookups return handles you can `tell`
and `ask` directly.

=== "Java"

    ```java
    public static final ServiceName<WorkerActor.Command> WORKERS =
            ServiceName.of(WorkerActor.Command.class, "workers");
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    val WORKERS: ServiceName<WorkerActor.Command> = ServiceName.of(WorkerActor.Command::class.java, "workers")
    ```

The id must not be blank. In cluster mode the messages must implement `JsonSerializable` or
`CborSerializable`, as for any message that crosses nodes.

## Registering

An actor can register itself when it starts, in its `withState` factory:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Component
    public class WorkerActor implements SpringActor<WorkerActor.Command> {

        public interface Command extends JsonSerializable {}

        public record DoJob(String jobId) implements Command {}

        @Override
        public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
            return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                    .withState(ctx -> {
                        ctx.registerWithReceptionist(WORKERS);
                        return ctx;
                    })
                    .onMessage(DoJob.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                        ctx.getLog().info("Running job {}", msg.jobId());
                        return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                    })
                    .build();
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @Component
    class WorkerActor : SpringActor<WorkerActor.Command> {

        sealed interface Command : JsonSerializable

        data class DoJob(val jobId: String) : Command

        override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
            actorBehavior<Command>(actorContext)
                .withState { ctx ->
                    ctx.registerWithReceptionist(WORKERS)
                    ctx
                }
                .onMessage(DoJob::class.java) { ctx, msg ->
                    ctx.log.info("Running job {}", msg.jobId)
                    SpringActorBehavior.same()
                }
                .build()
    }
    ```

Or any code can register an actor it has a ref to, with `receptionist.register(name, ref)`:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    SpringActorHandle<WorkerActor.Command> worker = actorSystem.actor(WorkerActor.class)
            .withId("worker-1")
            .spawnAndWait();
    receptionist.register(WORKERS, worker);
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    // In a suspend function
    val worker = actorSystem.actor<WorkerActor, _>().withId("worker-1").awaitSpawn()
    receptionist.register(WORKERS, worker)
    ```

A stopped actor is removed from its services automatically. To remove a running one, call
`receptionist.deregister(name, ref)`.

## Finding

`find(name)` returns the actors registered under the name right now. The set may be empty.

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Service
    public class JobDispatcher {
        private final SpringReceptionist receptionist;

        public JobDispatcher(SpringReceptionist receptionist) {
            this.receptionist = receptionist;
        }

        public CompletionStage<Integer> dispatch(String jobId) {
            return receptionist.find(WORKERS).thenApply(workers -> {
                workers.forEach(w -> w.tell(new WorkerActor.DoJob(jobId)));
                return workers.size();
            });
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @Service
    class JobDispatcher(private val receptionist: SpringReceptionist) {

        suspend fun dispatch(jobId: String): Int {
            val workers = receptionist.find(WORKERS).await()
            workers.forEach { it.tell(WorkerActor.DoJob(jobId)) }
            return workers.size
        }
    }
    ```

`find(name)` waits up to 3 seconds for the receptionist's answer; `find(name, timeout)` sets another
limit. The result is a `Set<SpringActorHandle<T>>`; each handle supports `tell` and `ask`.

## Subscribing to changes

`subscribe(name, listener)` calls the listener with the current set right away, then with the full new
set every time an actor registers, deregisters or stops:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    SpringReceptionistSubscription<WorkerActor.Command> subscription =
            receptionist.subscribe(WORKERS, workers -> log.info("{} workers available", workers.size()));

    // later, for example in a @PreDestroy method
    subscription.cancel();
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    val subscription: SpringReceptionistSubscription<WorkerActor.Command> =
        receptionist.subscribe(WORKERS) { workers -> log.info("{} workers available", workers.size) }

    // later, for example in a @PreDestroy method
    subscription.cancel()
    ```

- The listener runs on an actor thread. Keep it short and never block in it. A common pattern is to copy
  the set into a field (an `AtomicReference`) that request code reads.
- If the listener throws, the error is logged and the subscription stays.
- Each subscription is backed by a small helper actor. `cancel()` stops it and is safe to call twice;
  after `cancel()` returns, the listener isn't called again. `isCancelled()` tells whether it was
  cancelled, and `whenTerminated()` completes once the helper actor has stopped.

## Cluster mode

In a cluster, registrations are replicated to all nodes. `find` on node 2 can return an actor that runs
on node 1, and `tell` on the returned handle goes over the network.

!!! warning "Eventually consistent"
    Replication takes time. Right after an actor registers on one node, a lookup on another node can
    still return an empty or older set. Don't treat an empty result as final: retry with a bounded wait,
    or use `subscribe` and act when the actor appears.

Registrations of a node that leaves the cluster are removed once the node is removed from membership.

## API summary

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| `ServiceName.of(type, id)` | Creates a service name |
| `register(name, ref)` | Registers an actor under a name |
| `deregister(name, ref)` | Removes an actor from a name |
| `find(name)`, `find(name, timeout)` | One-time lookup; default timeout 3 s |
| `subscribe(name, listener)` | Calls the listener now and on every change; returns a cancellable subscription |
| `SpringBehaviorContext.registerWithReceptionist(name)` | Registers the current actor from inside it |

## Related

- [Actors](actors.md): finding actors by class and id
- [Pub/sub topics](pub-sub-topics.md): one message to many actors
- [Sharded actors](../cluster/sharded-actors.md): one actor per id across a cluster
- [Cluster formation](../cluster/cluster-formation.md): running a cluster

<!-- Source: https://seonwkim.github.io/actor-spring-boot-starter/guides/core/dispatchers/ -->

# Dispatchers and Mailboxes

A **dispatcher** is the thread pool that runs actors. When an actor has messages, the dispatcher gives it
a thread, the actor handles a batch of messages, and the thread moves on to another actor. Thousands of
actors share a few threads this way.

A **mailbox** is the queue an actor's messages wait in until it handles them.

Most actors need neither setting: the default dispatcher and the default (unbounded) mailbox fit
non-blocking work. Change them when an actor blocks, when a group of actors must not slow down the
others, or when a queue must not grow without bound.

## Choosing a dispatcher

| Work in the handler | Dispatcher |
|---|---|
| Non-blocking: in-memory state, `tell`, `ask` with `pipeToSelf` | Default (nothing to set) |
| Blocking I/O: JDBC/JPA, file I/O, blocking HTTP clients | `withBlockingDispatcher()` |
| Blocking I/O, many concurrent calls, Java 21 | The blocking dispatcher on [virtual threads](#virtual-threads) |
| A group of actors that must be isolated from the rest | A [custom dispatcher](#custom-dispatchers) |
| Work on a thread pool your application already manages | A dispatcher on a [Spring `Executor` bean](#spring-executor-beans) |

!!! danger "Never block on the default dispatcher"
    The default dispatcher has about as many threads as CPU cores. An actor that blocks there holds one
    of them, and a few blocking actors can stall every other actor in the application.

## Selecting a dispatcher

Choose the dispatcher when you spawn the actor:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    // Blocking work: Pekko's blocking I/O dispatcher
    actorSystem.actor(ReportActor.class)
            .withId("report-1")
            .withBlockingDispatcher()
            .spawn();

    // A dispatcher defined in configuration (see below)
    actorSystem.actor(ReportActor.class)
            .withId("report-2")
            .withDispatcherFromConfig("reports")
            .spawn();
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    // In a suspend function

    // Blocking work: Pekko's blocking I/O dispatcher
    actorSystem.actor<ReportActor, _>()
        .withId("report-1")
        .withBlockingDispatcher()
        .awaitSpawn()

    // A dispatcher defined in configuration (see below)
    actorSystem.actor<ReportActor, _>()
        .withId("report-2")
        .withDispatcherFromConfig("reports")
        .awaitSpawn()
    ```

Both the spawn builder and the child builder take every form (the child builder's shortcut methods and
the spawn builder's `withDispatcher(DispatcherConfig)` since 1.1.0):

| Shortcut | `DispatcherConfig` form | Runs the actor on |
|---|---|---|
| `withDefaultDispatcher()` (the default) | `withDispatcher(DispatcherConfig.defaultDispatcher())` | The default dispatcher |
| `withBlockingDispatcher()` | `withDispatcher(DispatcherConfig.blocking())` | Pekko's `default-blocking-io-dispatcher` |
| `withDispatcherFromConfig(name)` | `withDispatcher(DispatcherConfig.fromConfig(name))` | The dispatcher defined under `spring.actor.<name>` or `spring.actor.dispatchers.<name>` |
| `withDispatcherSameAsParent()` | `withDispatcher(DispatcherConfig.sameAsParent())` | The parent's dispatcher |

For a child actor:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    ctx.getSelf().child(ExportWorker.class)
            .withId("export-1")
            .withBlockingDispatcher()
            .spawn();
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    ctx.self.child<ExportWorker, _>()
        .withId("export-1")
        .withBlockingDispatcher()
        .spawn()
    ```

An unknown dispatcher name makes the spawn fail; the actor system keeps working.

## The blocking dispatcher

`withBlockingDispatcher()` uses Pekko's `default-blocking-io-dispatcher`, a thread pool meant for
blocking calls. Pekko gives it 16 threads by default. Its threads are separate from the default
dispatcher's, so blocking actors can only slow each other down. Change its size with raw Pekko keys:

```yaml
spring:
  actor:
    pekko:
      actor:
        default-blocking-io-dispatcher:
          thread-pool-executor:
            fixed-pool-size: 32
```

## Custom dispatchers

Define your own dispatcher under `spring.actor.<name>` with Pekko's dispatcher keys. Every key under
`spring.actor` that the starter doesn't know is passed to Pekko without the prefix, so
`spring.actor.my-dispatcher` becomes Pekko's `my-dispatcher` (see
[Configuration](../operations/configuration.md)). Then spawn with `withDispatcherFromConfig("my-dispatcher")`.

A fixed thread pool, for blocking work you want to keep apart from the rest:

```yaml
spring:
  actor:
    db-dispatcher:
      type: Dispatcher
      executor: thread-pool-executor
      thread-pool-executor:
        fixed-pool-size: 16
      throughput: 1
```

A fork-join pool, for CPU-heavy work you want to keep apart:

```yaml
spring:
  actor:
    cpu-dispatcher:
      type: Dispatcher
      executor: fork-join-executor
      fork-join-executor:
        parallelism-min: 2
        parallelism-factor: 1.0   # threads = CPU cores x factor, within min and max
        parallelism-max: 8
      throughput: 100
```

A thread pool that grows and shrinks:

```yaml
spring:
  actor:
    elastic-dispatcher:
      type: Dispatcher
      executor: thread-pool-executor
      thread-pool-executor:
        core-pool-size-min: 4
        core-pool-size-factor: 2.0
        core-pool-size-max: 16
        max-pool-size-min: 8
        max-pool-size-factor: 2.0
        max-pool-size-max: 32
      throughput: 10
```

Pekko also has `type: PinnedDispatcher`, which gives each actor its own thread. It uses one thread per
actor, so keep it for a handful of actors. All dispatcher keys are in the
[Pekko dispatcher documentation](https://pekko.apache.org/docs/pekko/current/typed/dispatchers.html).

### Throughput

`throughput` is the number of messages an actor may handle before its thread moves on to the next
actor. A high value (100) means fewer switches and more speed; a low value (1) is fairer, so one busy
actor can't keep others waiting. Use 1 for dispatchers whose actors block.

## Spring Executor beans

A dispatcher can run its actors on an `Executor` bean of your application, for example a
`ThreadPoolTaskExecutor` you already tune and monitor:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Bean
    ThreadPoolTaskExecutor reportExecutor() {
        ThreadPoolTaskExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
        executor.setThreadNamePrefix("reports-");
        executor.setCorePoolSize(8);
        return executor;
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @Bean
    fun reportExecutor(): ThreadPoolTaskExecutor = ThreadPoolTaskExecutor().apply {
        setThreadNamePrefix("reports-")
        corePoolSize = 8
    }
    ```

```yaml
spring:
  actor:
    dispatchers:
      reports:
        executor: reportExecutor   # the bean name
        throughput: 10             # optional
```

Spawn with `withDispatcherFromConfig("reports")`. The Spring context owns the executor: the actor system
never shuts it down, and it keeps running while the actor system stops.

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `spring.actor.dispatchers.<name>.executor` | The name of an `Executor` bean |
| `spring.actor.dispatchers.<name>.virtual` | `true` for a dispatcher on virtual threads (see below) |
| `spring.actor.dispatchers.<name>.throughput` | Optional throughput |

A dispatcher sets either `executor` or `virtual: true`, not both. The name may contain letters, digits,
`-` and `_`.

## Virtual threads

On Java 21, blocking actors can run on virtual threads: a blocked virtual thread doesn't hold a platform
thread, so many blocking calls can wait at once.

```yaml
spring:
  actor:
    virtual-threads:
      enabled: true            # auto (default) | true | false
    dispatchers:
      virtual-thread-dispatcher:
        virtual: true
```

- `spring.actor.virtual-threads.enabled` runs the blocking dispatcher (`withBlockingDispatcher()`) on
  virtual threads. The default, `auto`, follows Spring Boot's `spring.threads.virtual.enabled`, so an
  application that turns on virtual threads for Spring gets them for blocking actors too. `false` keeps
  platform threads even when Spring's flag is on.
- `spring.actor.dispatchers.<name>.virtual: true` defines a named dispatcher on virtual threads, whatever
  the switch says. Spawn with `withDispatcherFromConfig("<name>")`.
- The default dispatcher always stays on its platform fork-join pool: actors that never block gain
  nothing from virtual threads.
- A raw `spring.actor.pekko.actor.default-blocking-io-dispatcher.executor` still wins over the switch,
  with a warning in the log.

!!! warning "Pinning"
    A virtual thread that blocks inside a `synchronized` block, or in some native calls, pins its
    carrier (platform) thread until it unblocks, and too many pinned carriers stall every virtual thread.
    Use `java.util.concurrent` locks (`ReentrantLock`) around blocking calls, and find pinning with
    `-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=short`.

Virtual threads help blocking I/O, not CPU-heavy work. The JVM's own settings
(`jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism`, `jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize`) rarely need
changes. The [virtual-threads example](../../examples/virtual-threads.md) compares platform and virtual
threads on the same workload.

## Mailboxes

By default each actor has an unbounded mailbox: it accepts every message, and a slow actor's queue grows
until memory runs out. Set another mailbox when you spawn the actor:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    // At most 1,000 waiting messages; further messages go to dead letters
    actorSystem.actor(IngestActor.class)
            .withId("ingest")
            .withMailbox(MailboxConfig.bounded(1_000))
            .spawn();

    // A mailbox defined in configuration
    actorSystem.actor(IngestActor.class)
            .withId("ingest-priority")
            .withMailbox(MailboxConfig.fromConfig("priority-mailbox"))
            .spawn();
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    // In a suspend function

    // At most 1,000 waiting messages; further messages go to dead letters
    actorSystem.actor<IngestActor, _>()
        .withId("ingest")
        .withMailbox(MailboxConfig.bounded(1_000))
        .awaitSpawn()

    // A mailbox defined in configuration
    actorSystem.actor<IngestActor, _>()
        .withId("ingest-priority")
        .withMailbox(MailboxConfig.fromConfig("priority-mailbox"))
        .awaitSpawn()
    ```

| `MailboxConfig` | Mailbox |
|---|---|
| `defaultMailbox()` | Unbounded (the default) |
| `bounded(capacity)` | Holds at most `capacity` messages; messages beyond that are dropped to dead letters. `capacity` must be positive. |
| `fromConfig(name)` | The mailbox defined under `spring.actor.<name>` |

A mailbox from configuration names a Pekko mailbox class, for example a priority mailbox that handles
some messages before others:

```yaml
spring:
  actor:
    priority-mailbox:
      mailbox-type: com.example.PriorityMailbox
```

Pekko's priority mailboxes (`UnboundedPriorityMailbox`, `UnboundedStablePriorityMailbox`,
`BoundedPriorityMailbox`, `BoundedStablePriorityMailbox`) need a subclass that supplies the ordering;
see the [Pekko mailbox documentation](https://pekko.apache.org/docs/pekko/current/typed/mailboxes.html).

A bounded mailbox drops messages silently from the sender's point of view: `tell` still returns, and an
`ask` times out. Use it to protect memory, and make senders slow down (with ask, or with
[streams](../streaming/reactor-streams.md)) when you need back-pressure.

## Pitfalls

- **Blocking on the default dispatcher.** The most common cause of an application that stops responding
  under load.
- **One huge blocking pool for everything.** Give separate dispatchers to workloads that must not wait
  for each other (for example, the database and a slow partner API).
- **Unbounded mailboxes in front of slow actors.** Watch mailbox sizes (see
  [Monitoring](../operations/monitoring.md)) and bound the ones that can grow.
- **`virtual` and `executor` on one dispatcher.** The application fails to start; choose one.

## Related

- [Actors](actors.md): the spawn builder
- [Configuration](../operations/configuration.md): all `spring.actor` keys
- [Monitoring](../operations/monitoring.md): dispatcher and mailbox metrics
- [Virtual threads example](../../examples/virtual-threads.md)

---

<!-- Source: https://seonwkim.github.io/actor-spring-boot-starter/guides/core/logging/ -->

# Logging with MDC and Tags

Logs from actors are harder to follow than logs from request threads: one actor handles messages for
many requests, and one request can pass through several actors. The starter gives you three ways to put
context on every log line an actor writes:

- **Static MDC**: key-value pairs fixed when the actor is spawned (a user id, a service name).
- **Dynamic MDC**: key-value pairs computed from each message (an order id, a request id).
- **Tags**: labels on an actor (`worker`, `critical`), written to the `pekkoTags` field.

MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) is SLF4J's map of values that the log pattern can print with `%X{key}`.

Inside actors, log through the actor's logger, `ctx.getLog()` (`ctx.log` in Kotlin): its lines carry the
fields below and the actor's MDC.

## Fields Pekko adds

Every line written through `ctx.getLog()` already carries these MDC fields:

| Field | Value | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `pekkoSource` | The actor's path | `pekko://my-app/user/...` |
| `pekkoAddress` | The actor system's address | `pekko://my-app@10.0.0.5:25520` |
| `pekkoTags` | The actor's tags, comma-separated | `worker,high-priority` |
| `sourceActorSystem` | The actor system's name | `my-app` |

## Static MDC

Set values that stay the same for the actor's whole life when you spawn it:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    actorSystem.actor(SessionActor.class)
            .withId("session-" + sessionId)
            .withMdc(MdcConfig.of(Map.of(
                    "sessionId", sessionId,
                    "userId", userId)))
            .spawn();
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    // In a suspend function
    actorSystem.actor<SessionActor, _>()
        .withId("session-$sessionId")
        .withMdc(MdcConfig.of(mapOf("sessionId" to sessionId, "userId" to userId)))
        .awaitSpawn()
    ```

Every line the actor logs then carries `sessionId` and `userId`. `MdcConfig.of` needs at least one entry;
`MdcConfig.empty()` means none.

## Dynamic MDC

Compute values from each message with `withMdc` on the behavior builder. The function receives every
message and returns the map for the time that message is handled:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Component
    public class OrderProcessorActor implements SpringActor<OrderProcessorActor.Command> {

        public interface Command {}

        public record ProcessOrder(String orderId, String userId, String requestId) implements Command {}

        @Override
        public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
            return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                    .withMdc(msg -> {
                        if (msg instanceof ProcessOrder order) {
                            Map<String, String> mdc = new HashMap<>();
                            mdc.put("orderId", order.orderId());
                            mdc.put("userId", order.userId());
                            if (order.requestId() != null) {   // MDC values must not be null
                                mdc.put("requestId", order.requestId());
                            }
                            return mdc;
                        }
                        return Map.of();
                    })
                    .onMessage(ProcessOrder.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                        ctx.getLog().info("Processing order");   // carries orderId, userId, requestId
                        return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                    })
                    .build();
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @Component
    class OrderProcessorActor : SpringActor<OrderProcessorActor.Command> {

        sealed interface Command

        data class ProcessOrder(val orderId: String, val userId: String, val requestId: String?) : Command

        override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
            actorBehavior<Command>(actorContext)
                .withMdc { msg ->
                    when (msg) {
                        is ProcessOrder -> buildMap {
                            put("orderId", msg.orderId)
                            put("userId", msg.userId)
                            msg.requestId?.let { put("requestId", it) }   // MDC values must not be null
                        }
                    }
                }
                .onMessage(ProcessOrder::class.java) { ctx, _ ->
                    ctx.log.info("Processing order")   // carries orderId, userId, requestId
                    SpringActorBehavior.same()
                }
                .build()
    }
    ```

Return an empty map for messages without context. Static and dynamic MDC combine: a line carries both the
spawn-time values and the values of the current message.

### Carrying a request id into an actor

The MDC of the thread that sends a message does not travel with the message: the actor runs on another
thread. To see a request id in the actor's logs, read it on the sending side, put it in the message, and
add it back with `withMdc`. The [logging example](../../examples/logging.md) does this: a `WebFilter`
puts `requestId` in the MDC of the request, the service reads it and passes it in `ProcessOrder`, and the
actor's `withMdc` (above) puts it on the actor's lines.

=== "Java"

    ```java
    public Mono<OrderProcessed> processOrder(String userId) {
        String requestId = MDC.get("requestId");      // on the request thread
        String orderId = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        return Mono.fromCompletionStage(actorSystem.getOrSpawn(OrderProcessorActor.class, "order-processor")
                .thenCompose(actor -> actor
                        .ask(new OrderProcessorActor.ProcessOrder(orderId, userId, requestId))
                        .execute()));
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    suspend fun processOrder(userId: String): OrderProcessed {
        val requestId = MDC.get("requestId")          // read before the first suspension point
        val orderId = UUID.randomUUID().toString()
        return actorSystem.awaitGetOrSpawn<OrderProcessorActor, _>("order-processor")
            .awaitAsk(OrderProcessorActor.ProcessOrder(orderId, userId, requestId))
    }
    ```

(Here `ProcessOrder` is an `AskCommand<OrderProcessed>`, as in the example.) With Micrometer Tracing on,
the trace itself travels with messages, and lines carry `traceId` and `spanId`; see
[Monitoring](../operations/monitoring.md#tracing).

## Tags

Tags label an actor by role, priority or workload. They are written to the `pekkoTags` field of every
line, so you can filter on them:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    actorSystem.actor(PaymentProcessor.class)
            .withId("payment-processor")
            .withTags(TagsConfig.of("payment-service", "critical"))
            .spawn();
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    // In a suspend function
    actorSystem.actor<PaymentProcessor, _>()
        .withId("payment-processor")
        .withTags(TagsConfig.of("payment-service", "critical"))
        .awaitSpawn()
    ```

`TagsConfig.of(...)` takes one or more strings or a `Set<String>`; `TagsConfig.empty()` means none.
Duplicate tags count once.

## Children

The child builder has the same `withMdc` and `withTags`. A child does not inherit its parent's MDC or
tags; give it its own:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    ctx.getSelf().child(WorkerActor.class)
            .withId("worker-1")
            .withTags(TagsConfig.of("worker"))
            .withMdc(MdcConfig.of(Map.of("parentId", actorContext.actorId())))
            .spawn();
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    ctx.self.child<WorkerActor, _>()
        .withId("worker-1")
        .withTags(TagsConfig.of("worker"))
        .withMdc(MdcConfig.of(mapOf("parentId" to actorContext.actorId())))
        .spawn()
    ```

## Printing MDC with Logback

MDC values appear only if the log pattern prints them. A console pattern:

```xml
<configuration>
    <appender name="CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder>
            <pattern>%d{ISO8601} %-5level [%X{pekkoSource}] [%X{pekkoTags}] [reqId=%X{requestId}] [userId=%X{userId}] %logger{36} - %msg%n</pattern>
        </encoder>
    </appender>

    <root level="INFO">
        <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/>
    </root>
</configuration>
```

For log aggregation (Elasticsearch, Loki), write JSON with the
[Logstash encoder](https://github.com/logfellow/logstash-logback-encoder) and list the MDC keys to
include:

```xml
<appender name="JSON" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
    <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder">
        <includeMdcKeyName>pekkoSource</includeMdcKeyName>
        <includeMdcKeyName>pekkoTags</includeMdcKeyName>
        <includeMdcKeyName>requestId</includeMdcKeyName>
        <includeMdcKeyName>userId</includeMdcKeyName>
        <includeMdcKeyName>orderId</includeMdcKeyName>
        <includeMdcKeyName>traceId</includeMdcKeyName>
        <includeMdcKeyName>spanId</includeMdcKeyName>
    </encoder>
</appender>
```

It needs `net.logstash.logback:logstash-logback-encoder` on the classpath. In production, put file and
JSON appenders behind Logback's `AsyncAppender` so that writing a log line never makes an actor wait on
disk. The logging example's
[`logback.xml`](https://github.com/seonWKim/actor-spring-boot-starter/tree/main/example/logging/src/main/resources/logback.xml)
has console, rolling file and JSON appenders, each async.

## Good practice

- Use the same MDC key names everywhere (`userId`, `requestId`, `orderId`), so one query finds a request
  across services and actors.
- Keep the number of keys small; every key is copied for every message.
- Never put secrets or personal data (passwords, card numbers, tokens) in MDC or tags.
- Use tags for what an actor *is* (role, service, priority) and MDC for what it is *working on*.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| MDC keys are empty in the output | The pattern has no `%X{key}` for them, or the line was logged outside the actor's handler (for example in a future callback) |
| `requestId` missing in actor logs | Thread MDC doesn't follow messages; pass the id in the message and add it with `withMdc` |
| `pekkoTags` empty | The actor was spawned without `withTags(...)`, or the pattern lacks `%X{pekkoTags}` |

## Related

- [Actors](actors.md): the spawn and child builders
- [Behaviors](behaviors.md): the behavior builder
- [Monitoring](../operations/monitoring.md): metrics, tracing and log setup in production
- [Logging example](../../examples/logging.md)
- [Pekko logging](https://pekko.apache.org/docs/pekko/current/typed/logging.html)
