<!-- Source: https://seonwkim.github.io/actor-spring-boot-starter/guides/cluster/sharded-actors/ -->

# Sharded Actors

A sharded actor is an actor type whose instances, called **entities**, are spread over the nodes of a
cluster. Each entity has an id. The cluster runs at most one entity per id at a time, starts it on its
first message, and moves it when nodes join or leave. You send a message to an id from any node, and it
reaches the entity wherever it runs.

Use sharding when you have many things that each need their own actor: users, orders, devices, chat
rooms. It spreads them over the nodes, so you scale out by adding nodes.

For one actor for the whole cluster, use a [cluster singleton](singletons.md) instead. For actors that
live on one node only, use regular actors ([Actors](../core/actors.md)).

## Setup

Sharded actors need the cluster starter:

=== "Gradle"

    ```kotlin
    implementation("io.github.seonwkim:actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster:$version")
    ```

=== "Maven"

    ```xml
    <dependency>
        <groupId>io.github.seonwkim</groupId>
        <artifactId>actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster</artifactId>
        <version>${actor.version}</version>
    </dependency>
    ```

Then run the actor system in cluster mode. This is the configuration of the
[cluster example](../../examples/cluster.md), three nodes on one machine:

```yaml
spring:
  actor:
    name: spring-pekko-example
    provider: cluster
    remote:
      hostname: 127.0.0.1
      port: 2551
    cluster:
      seed-nodes:
        - pekko://spring-pekko-example@127.0.0.1:2551
        - pekko://spring-pekko-example@127.0.0.1:2552
        - pekko://spring-pekko-example@127.0.0.1:2553
      downing:
        strategy: keep-majority
```

Each node uses its own `remote.port` (2551, 2552, 2553) and the same `spring.actor.name`. See
[Cluster Formation](cluster-formation.md) for joining without fixed addresses, and
[Split Brain and Leases](split-brain-and-leases.md) for the downing strategy.

## Write a sharded actor

Implement `SpringShardedActor` and annotate the class with `@Component`. The starter registers every
sharded actor bean with the cluster when the actor system starts.

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Component
    public class HelloActor implements SpringShardedActor<HelloActor.Command> {

        public static final ShardedEntityType<Command> TYPE_KEY =
                ShardedEntityType.of(Command.class, "HelloActor");

        public interface Command extends JsonSerializable {}

        public static class SayHello extends AskCommand<String> implements Command {
            public final String message;

            public SayHello(String message) {
                this.message = message;
            }
        }

        @Override
        public ShardedEntityType<Command> entityType() {
            return TYPE_KEY;
        }

        @Override
        public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringShardedActorContext<Command> ctx) {
            String entityId = ctx.getEntityId();
            return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, ctx)
                    .onMessage(SayHello.class, (behaviorCtx, msg) -> {
                        String reply = "Received from entity [" + entityId + "] on node ["
                                + behaviorCtx.nodeAddress() + "]";
                        behaviorCtx.getLog().info(reply);
                        msg.reply(reply);
                        return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                    })
                    .build();
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @Component
    class HelloActor : SpringShardedActor<HelloActor.Command> {

        companion object {
            val TYPE_KEY: ShardedEntityType<Command> = ShardedEntityType.of(Command::class.java, "HelloActor")
        }

        sealed interface Command : JsonSerializable

        class SayHello(val message: String) : AskCommand<String>(), Command

        override fun entityType(): ShardedEntityType<Command> = TYPE_KEY

        override fun create(ctx: SpringShardedActorContext<Command>): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
            val entityId = ctx.entityId
            return actorBehavior<Command>(ctx)
                .onMessage(SayHello::class.java) { behaviorCtx, msg ->
                    val reply = "Received from entity [$entityId] on node [${behaviorCtx.nodeAddress()}]"
                    behaviorCtx.log.info(reply)
                    msg.reply(reply)
                    SpringActorBehavior.same()
                }
                .build()
        }
    }
    ```

What differs from a regular actor:

| Part | What it does |
|---|---|
| `ShardedEntityType.of(Command.class, "HelloActor")` | Names the entity type and its message type. Nodes reach the same entities when they use the same name, so keep it stable across deployments. |
| `entityType()` | Returns that type. |
| `create(SpringShardedActorContext<T>)` | Builds the behavior of one entity, on the node that hosts it. `ctx.getEntityId()` is the entity's id (also `ctx.actorId()`), and the same `SpringActorBehavior` builder works as for a regular actor, `withState` included. |
| `sharding()` | Optional: how ids map to shards. Default `ShardingStrategy.defaults()`, 100 shards. |
| `role()` | Optional: the cluster role whose nodes host the entities. Default: every node. |

Messages cross the network, so the command interface extends `JsonSerializable` (or `CborSerializable`),
and so do the replies when they are not `String` or a number.

## Send messages

`actorSystem.sharded(HelloActor.class).withId(id).get()` returns a handle to the entity with that id. Getting
a handle does not start the entity and costs nearly nothing: the entity starts on its first message.

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Service
    public class HelloService {

        private final SpringActorSystem actorSystem;

        public HelloService(SpringActorSystem actorSystem) {
            this.actorSystem = actorSystem;
        }

        public Mono<String> hello(String message, String entityId) {
            SpringShardedActorHandle<HelloActor.Command> entity =
                    actorSystem.sharded(HelloActor.class).withId(entityId).get();

            CompletionStage<String> reply = entity
                    .ask(new HelloActor.SayHello(message))
                    .withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
                    .onTimeout(() -> "Request timed out for entity: " + entityId)
                    .execute();

            return Mono.fromCompletionStage(reply);
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @Service
    class HelloService(private val actorSystem: SpringActorSystem) {

        suspend fun hello(message: String, entityId: String): String {
            val entity = actorSystem.sharded<HelloActor, _>().withId(entityId).get()
            return entity.ask(HelloActor.SayHello(message))
                .withTimeout(3.seconds)
                .onTimeout { "Request timed out for entity: $entityId" }
                .await()
        }
    }
    ```

The handle has `tell`, `ask`, `entityId()` and `entityType()`. `withTimeout` on the builder sets the default
ask timeout of the handle (3 seconds otherwise).

There is no `spawn`, `exists` or `stop` for an entity, and no need to cache handles: get one per request.

| | Regular actor | Sharded entity |
|---|---|---|
| Created | By you, with `spawn()` or `getOrSpawn()` | By the cluster, on its first message |
| Where it runs | The node that spawned it | One node of the cluster, chosen by its shard |
| How many per id | One per node | One per cluster |
| Handle | From `spawn`, `get` or `getOrSpawn` | From `sharded(...).withId(id).get()`, any time |
| Messages | Any Java object | Serializable (`JsonSerializable`, `CborSerializable`) |

## Shards and ids

Entities are grouped into shards: a hash of the entity id picks the shard, and the cluster places whole
shards on nodes. When a node joins or leaves, shards move, and their entities start again on their new node
on the next message.

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Override
    public ShardingStrategy sharding() {
        return ShardingStrategy.hashed(300);
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    override fun sharding(): ShardingStrategy = ShardingStrategy.hashed(300)
    ```

- Use about ten times the largest number of nodes you expect. The default is 100.
- Every node must use the same strategy for an entity type, and it must stay the same across deployments:
  a different number of shards sends the same id to a different shard.
- Pick ids with many distinct values, such as user ids or order numbers, so the entities spread evenly.

## Run entities on some nodes only

Override `role()` and give the hosting nodes that role:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Override
    public Optional<String> role() {
        return Optional.of("backend");
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    override fun role(): Optional<String> = Optional.of("backend")
    ```

```yaml
spring:
  actor:
    cluster:
      roles: [backend]
```

Nodes without the role still send messages to the entities, through a proxy; they just don't host any.

## State and passivation

An entity's state lives in memory. It is lost when the entity stops: when its shard moves to another node,
when its node stops, or when the entity is passivated.

Passivation is Pekko's: an entity that receives no message for a while is stopped to free memory, and
started again on its next message. Pekko's default idle timeout is 2 minutes. Change it with the raw key:

```yaml
spring:
  actor:
    pekko:
      cluster:
        sharding:
          passivation:
            default-idle-strategy:
              idle-entity:
                timeout: 10m
```

When the state must survive, load it when the entity starts and save it when it changes, as in
[State in a Database](../data/state-in-a-database.md), or use an
[event-sourced actor](../data/event-sourcing.md).

## One entity per id, even in a split

In a network split, both sides may start the same shard. A downing strategy stops one side; with
`spring.actor.cluster.sharding.use-lease: true`, each shard also takes a lease before it starts its
entities, so a shard never runs on two nodes. See [Split Brain and Leases](split-brain-and-leases.md#leases).

## Monitoring

With `actor-metrics` and Micrometer, each node reports `actor.sharding.regions`, `actor.sharding.shards` and
`actor.sharding.entities`, tagged `type` with the entity type name. The `actors` Actuator endpoint lists,
for each entity type, the regions and the shards and entities on this node. See
[Monitoring](../operations/monitoring.md).

## Pitfalls

- **Unstable names or shard counts.** Renaming the entity type or changing the number of shards sends
  existing ids to other entities. Keep both fixed.
- **Blocking in an entity.** Entities run on the default dispatcher. Use a non-blocking client, or hand
  the blocking call off and send the result back with `pipeToSelf` (see
  [State in a Database](../data/state-in-a-database.md#non-blocking-calls-with-r2dbc)).
- **Many messages between entities.** Every message to another entity may cross the network. Keep what is
  used together in one entity.
- **Holding state only in memory.** It is gone after passivation or a move. Store what must survive.

## Related

- [Cluster example](../../examples/cluster.md): sharded actors on three nodes
- [Cluster Singletons](singletons.md): one actor for the whole cluster
- [Split Brain and Leases](split-brain-and-leases.md): downing and shard leases
- [State in a Database](../data/state-in-a-database.md) and [Event-Sourced Actors](../data/event-sourcing.md):
  keep an entity's state
- [Testing](../testing.md#cluster-tests-with-actorcluster): several nodes in one test

<!-- Source: https://seonwkim.github.io/actor-spring-boot-starter/guides/cluster/singletons/ -->

# Cluster Singletons

A cluster singleton is an actor that runs on exactly one node of the cluster. Every node can send it
messages through a proxy, and when the node that runs it leaves or fails, the singleton starts again on
another node.

Use a singleton for work that must happen once for the whole cluster:

- a coordinator that hands out work or ids,
- a scheduler that runs a job every few minutes,
- an aggregator that collects numbers from every node,
- a cluster-wide limit, such as a rate limiter shared by all nodes.

Don't use one for work that grows with your traffic. A singleton is one actor on one node: every message
for it goes through that node, one at a time. For many independent things (users, orders, devices), use
[sharded actors](sharded-actors.md) instead: one entity per id, spread over the nodes.

## Setup

Singletons need the cluster starter and cluster mode:

=== "Gradle"

    ```kotlin
    implementation("io.github.seonwkim:actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster:$version")
    ```

=== "Maven"

    ```xml
    <dependency>
        <groupId>io.github.seonwkim</groupId>
        <artifactId>actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster</artifactId>
        <version>${actor.version}</version>
    </dependency>
    ```

```yaml
spring:
  actor:
    name: orders
    provider: cluster
    remote:
      hostname: 127.0.0.1
      port: 2551
    cluster:
      seed-nodes:
        - pekko://orders@127.0.0.1:2551
        - pekko://orders@127.0.0.1:2552
      downing:
        strategy: keep-majority
```

See [Cluster Formation](cluster-formation.md) for how nodes find each other, and
[Split Brain and Leases](split-brain-and-leases.md) for the downing strategy.

## Write the actor

A singleton is a regular actor. Nothing in the class says it is a singleton: you choose that when you
spawn it. Its messages cross the network, so they must be serializable (`JsonSerializable` or
`CborSerializable`), the same as for sharded actors.

This one is adapted from the
[cluster example](https://github.com/seonWKim/actor-spring-boot-starter/tree/main/example/cluster):

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Component
    public class ClusterMetricsAggregator implements SpringActor<ClusterMetricsAggregator.Command> {

        public interface Command extends JsonSerializable {}

        public static class RecordMetric implements Command {
            public final String nodeAddress;
            public final String metricName;
            public final long value;

            public RecordMetric(String nodeAddress, String metricName, long value) {
                this.nodeAddress = nodeAddress;
                this.metricName = metricName;
                this.value = value;
            }
        }

        public static class GetTotal extends AskCommand<Long> implements Command {
            public final String metricName;

            public GetTotal(String metricName) {
                this.metricName = metricName;
            }
        }

        @Override
        public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
            Map<String, Long> totals = new HashMap<>();
            return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                    .onMessage(RecordMetric.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                        totals.merge(msg.metricName, msg.value, Long::sum);
                        return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                    })
                    .onMessage(GetTotal.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                        msg.reply(totals.getOrDefault(msg.metricName, 0L));
                        return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                    })
                    .build();
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @Component
    class ClusterMetricsAggregator : SpringActor<ClusterMetricsAggregator.Command> {

        sealed interface Command : JsonSerializable

        class RecordMetric(val nodeAddress: String, val metricName: String, val value: Long) : Command

        class GetTotal(val metricName: String) : AskCommand<Long>(), Command

        override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
            val totals = mutableMapOf<String, Long>()
            return actorBehavior<Command>(actorContext)
                .onMessage(RecordMetric::class.java) { _, msg ->
                    totals.merge(msg.metricName, msg.value, Long::plus)
                    SpringActorBehavior.same()
                }
                .onMessage(GetTotal::class.java) { _, msg ->
                    msg.reply(totals.getOrDefault(msg.metricName, 0L))
                    SpringActorBehavior.same()
                }
                .build()
        }
    }
    ```

## Spawn it

Call `asClusterSingleton()` on the spawn builder:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    SpringActorHandle<ClusterMetricsAggregator.Command> aggregator = actorSystem
            .actor(ClusterMetricsAggregator.class)
            .withId("metrics-aggregator")
            .asClusterSingleton()
            .spawn()
            .toCompletableFuture()
            .get();
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    // In a suspend fun or a coroutine
    val aggregator: SpringActorHandle<ClusterMetricsAggregator.Command> = actorSystem
        .actor<ClusterMetricsAggregator, _>()
        .withId("metrics-aggregator")
        .asClusterSingleton()
        .awaitSpawn()
    ```

`asClusterSingleton(boolean)` does the same with a flag, for code that decides at run time.

What you get back is a handle to a **proxy** on this node, not to the actor itself. The proxy finds the
node that runs the singleton and forwards every message there. `tell` and `ask` work as on any handle.

Every node spawns the singleton with the same class and id. The class name and the id form the singleton's
name (`<class name>:<id>`), and nodes that use the same name share one singleton. Spawning it again, on the
same node or another one, is safe: it returns a proxy to the same singleton and does not start a second
one.

The usual place is a bean that spawns it once at startup and keeps the handle:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Service
    public class ClusterSingletonService {

        private final SpringActorSystem actorSystem;
        private SpringActorHandle<ClusterMetricsAggregator.Command> aggregator;

        public ClusterSingletonService(SpringActorSystem actorSystem) {
            this.actorSystem = actorSystem;
        }

        @PostConstruct
        public void init() throws Exception {
            aggregator = actorSystem
                    .actor(ClusterMetricsAggregator.class)
                    .withId("metrics-aggregator")
                    .asClusterSingleton()
                    .spawn()
                    .toCompletableFuture()
                    .get();
        }

        public void record(String name, long value) {
            aggregator.tell(new ClusterMetricsAggregator.RecordMetric(actorSystem.nodeAddress(), name, value));
        }

        public CompletionStage<Long> total(String name) {
            return aggregator
                    .ask(new ClusterMetricsAggregator.GetTotal(name))
                    .withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
                    .execute();
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @Service
    class ClusterSingletonService(private val actorSystem: SpringActorSystem) {

        private lateinit var aggregator: SpringActorHandle<ClusterMetricsAggregator.Command>

        @PostConstruct
        fun init() {
            aggregator = actorSystem
                .actor<ClusterMetricsAggregator, _>()
                .withId("metrics-aggregator")
                .asClusterSingleton()
                .spawn()
                .toCompletableFuture()
                .get()
        }

        fun record(name: String, value: Long) {
            aggregator.tell(ClusterMetricsAggregator.RecordMetric(actorSystem.nodeAddress(), name, value))
        }

        suspend fun total(name: String): Long =
            aggregator.awaitAsk(ClusterMetricsAggregator.GetTotal(name), timeout = 3.seconds)
    }
    ```

The proxy stays valid for the life of the node, also when the singleton moves. Keep it and reuse it.

The other spawn settings apply to the singleton: `withSupervisionStrategy`, the dispatcher
(`withBlockingDispatcher()`, `withDispatcherFromConfig(...)`), the mailbox and tags.

!!! warning "`find` and `exists` see only singletons this node spawned"
    `actorSystem.find(...)` and `exists(...)` find a singleton on the nodes that called `spawn()` with
    `asClusterSingleton()` for it. On another node they report no actor: call `spawn()` with
    `asClusterSingleton()` there too (it is idempotent), or `getOrSpawn()`. A child actor can't be a
    singleton: only actors spawned from `SpringActorSystem` can.

In local mode (`spring.actor.provider` not `cluster`), the stage returned by `spawn()` fails with
`IllegalStateException`: "Cluster singleton requested but cluster mode is not enabled. Set
spring.actor.provider=cluster and depend on io.github.seonwkim:actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster."

### Stopping

`stop()` on a singleton's handle throws `UnsupportedOperationException`, and the singleton and the handle
keep working. The handle is this node's proxy: stopping it would not stop the singleton, only cut this
node off from it, and every later `spawn()` on the node would get the same stopped proxy back. A singleton
runs as long as the cluster does.

## Where it runs

The singleton runs on the **oldest member** of the cluster whose status is `Up`: the node that joined
first. The other nodes run only a proxy.

| When | What happens |
|---|---|
| A node joins | Nothing. The oldest node keeps the singleton. |
| The host shuts down gracefully (`SIGTERM`, `context.close()`) | It leaves the cluster, the singleton stops there and starts on the next oldest node. |
| The host crashes or stops answering | The singleton starts on another node only after the host is downed and removed. That needs a downing strategy; without one, the singleton waits until you remove the node by hand. |
| No node is `Up` yet | Messages wait in the proxy until a host is up. |

While the singleton moves, the proxies keep the messages sent to it and deliver them once the new
instance runs. Pekko's proxy keeps up to 1000 messages per node and drops what doesn't fit; set
`spring.actor.pekko.cluster.singleton-proxy.buffer-size` to change it. An `ask` whose reply doesn't come
back in time fails with its timeout, or returns its `onTimeout` value.

### State is lost when it moves

The new instance is a new actor: it starts from `create(...)` with empty state. In the example above, the
totals start again from zero. If the singleton must keep its state, store it:

- load it in `withState(...)` from a table and save it after each change, as in
  [State in a Database](../data/state-in-a-database.md), or
- make the singleton an [event-sourced actor](../data/event-sourcing.md), which rebuilds its state from
  its stored events wherever it starts.

### Limit it to some nodes

To run singletons only on some nodes, give those nodes a role with `spring.actor.cluster.roles` and set
`spring.actor.cluster.singleton.role` on **every** node:

```yaml
# Nodes that may run singletons
spring:
  actor:
    cluster:
      roles: [backend]
      singleton:
        role: backend
```

```yaml
# Other nodes: no role, same singleton.role
spring:
  actor:
    cluster:
      singleton:
        role: backend
```

The singleton then runs on the oldest `Up` node with that role. Every node still gets a proxy, and the
nodes without the role still spawn it, as in [Spawn it](#spawn-it). Set the same `singleton.role` on every
node, so all proxies look for the same host. The role applies to every singleton of the application,
including the ones the starter starts for [projections](../data/projections.md).

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `spring.actor.cluster.singleton.role` | none | Singletons run only on nodes with this role. Sets Pekko's `pekko.cluster.singleton.role`. |

A sharded actor picks its role in code (`role()` on the actor, see
[Sharded Actors](sharded-actors.md#run-entities-on-some-nodes-only)). A singleton's role is one setting for
the node instead, because Pekko places all singletons of a node by the same role and the
`actor.cluster.singleton.host` gauge reports one host for all of them.

## Leases: never two at once

A singleton runs on one node only as long as the nodes agree on who is in the cluster. In a network split,
each side may see itself as the oldest and start its own singleton. The
[downing strategy](split-brain-and-leases.md#downing-strategy) stops one side, but it takes some time.

When two copies would do harm (two schedulers sending the same email, two coordinators handing out the
same id), turn on the singleton lease:

```yaml
spring:
  actor:
    cluster:
      singleton:
        use-lease: true
      lease:
        store: jdbc        # or redis, or custom (your LeaseStore bean)
```

The singleton then starts only after it takes its lease from the store, and stops when it loses it. A node
that can't get the lease keeps retrying, and the singleton does not run on that node meanwhile. Each
singleton has its own lease; its name starts with `<spring.actor.name>-singleton-` and ends with the
singleton's name, such as `orders-singleton-...:metrics-aggregator`. The owner is the node address.

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `spring.actor.cluster.singleton.use-lease` | `false` | A singleton runs only while it holds its lease. |
| `spring.actor.cluster.lease.store` | none | Where leases live: `jdbc`, `redis` or `custom`. Required with `use-lease`. |
| `spring.actor.cluster.lease.ttl` | `120s` | How long a lease stays held after its last renewal. |
| `spring.actor.cluster.lease.renew-interval` | `12s` | How often the holder renews it. |
| `spring.actor.cluster.lease.expiry-margin` | `10s` | The holder stops this long before the ttl runs out. |

The ttl also bounds how long a singleton can stay down after a crash: another node can take the lease only
once the crashed node's lease has expired. Pekko's `spring.actor.pekko.cluster.singleton.lease-retry-interval`
sets how often a node retries a refused lease.

With `store: redis`, a lease can be lost in a Redis failover, and two nodes can hold it for a moment. Use
`jdbc` when a singleton must never run twice. See [Leases](split-brain-and-leases.md#leases) for the stores,
the tables and your own `LeaseStore`.

## See where it runs

With `actor-metrics` and Micrometer, every node reports the gauge `actor.cluster.singleton.host`: `1` on the
node that runs the singletons, `0` on the others. Summed over the nodes it should be `1`. The Prometheus
rules in [`monitoring/`](https://github.com/seonWKim/actor-spring-boot-starter/tree/main/monitoring) alert
with `ActorClusterSingletonMissing` when the sum stays below `1` for 5 minutes.

The gauge means "this node is the oldest `Up` member with the singleton role" (any member when
`singleton.role` is not set). It does not look at the lease: with `use-lease`, the host it names may still
be waiting for its lease.

The `actors` Actuator endpoint (`/actuator/actors`, when exposed) shows the same flag in this node's view of
the cluster.

## Singletons the starter starts

Each [projection](../data/projections.md) runs as a cluster singleton in cluster mode, so one node handles
its events. Its singleton is named `projection-<name>`.

## Pitfalls

- **One node does all the work.** Keep the work a singleton does small, or have it hand work out to
  sharded entities or routers.
- **Blocking calls.** A singleton that calls a database or an HTTP service should run on the blocking
  dispatcher (`withBlockingDispatcher()`), like any blocking actor.
- **No downing strategy.** Without one, a crashed host keeps the singleton until someone removes the node.
  The starter logs a warning at startup when no downing strategy is set.
- **Different ids on different nodes.** Nodes that spawn with another id start another singleton.
- **State in memory.** It is gone when the singleton moves. Store what must survive.

## Related

- [Sharded Actors](sharded-actors.md): one actor per id, spread over the nodes
- [Split Brain and Leases](split-brain-and-leases.md): downing strategies and lease stores
- [Cluster Formation](cluster-formation.md): how nodes join
- [Cluster example](../../examples/cluster.md): a singleton aggregator you can run on three nodes and fail over
- [Monitoring](../operations/monitoring.md): the cluster meters and alerts

<!-- Source: https://seonwkim.github.io/actor-spring-boot-starter/guides/cluster/cluster-formation/ -->

# Cluster Formation

A node joins a cluster in one of two ways, set by `spring.actor.cluster.join`:

| `join` | How the node finds the cluster | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| `seed-nodes` (default) | The addresses in `spring.actor.cluster.seed-nodes` | Nodes have fixed addresses |
| `discovery` | Peers found through `spring.actor.cluster.discovery.method`, then Pekko Cluster Bootstrap forms or joins the cluster | Nodes come and go with changing addresses (Kubernetes, autoscaling groups) |

## Joining through a store you already run

With `discovery.method` set to `jdbc` or `redis`, each node writes its own entry to a table or a Redis key,
and reads the others' entries to find its peers. This needs no Kubernetes API access (no RBAC) and no DNS
setup: only the store the application already uses, and network access between the nodes.

What each node does:

1. At startup it registers itself (its management host and the port its management server bound) and starts
   Cluster Bootstrap.
2. Every `heartbeat-interval` (default `5s`) it renews its entry.
3. Bootstrap lists the entries renewed within `ttl` (default `30s`), contacts those nodes on their management
   port, and either joins the cluster they are in or, if there is none yet, the node with the lowest address
   forms it.
4. On a graceful shutdown it deletes its entry first, so new nodes no longer contact it. A node that crashes
   stops renewing, and its entry is ignored once it is older than the ttl.

Times come from the store's clock (the database's `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`, Redis `TIME`), so the nodes' clocks
need not agree.

### Dependencies

Discovery uses Pekko Cluster Bootstrap and the management HTTP server, plus the module of your store:

=== "Gradle"

    ```kotlin
    implementation("io.github.seonwkim:actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster:$version")
    implementation("org.apache.pekko:pekko-management-cluster-bootstrap_3:1.1.1")
    implementation("org.apache.pekko:pekko-management-cluster-http_3:1.1.1")
    implementation("io.github.seonwkim:actor-jdbc:$version")   // or actor-redis
    ```

=== "Maven"

    ```xml
    <dependency>
        <groupId>io.github.seonwkim</groupId>
        <artifactId>actor-jdbc</artifactId> <!-- or actor-redis -->
        <version>${actor.version}</version>
    </dependency>
    ```

`actor-jdbc` uses the application's `DataSource`, and `actor-redis` its `RedisConnectionFactory`
(`spring-boot-starter-data-redis`).

### JDBC

```yaml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/orders
  actor:
    name: orders
    provider: cluster
    cluster:
      join: discovery
      discovery:
        method: jdbc
    jdbc:
      initialize-schema: always   # default: embedded (only H2, HSQLDB, Derby)
    pekko:
      management:
        http:
          port: 7626
```

The entries live in the `actor_peer` table. `spring.actor.jdbc.initialize-schema` decides when the starter creates it:
`embedded` (the default) only in an embedded database, `always`, or `never`. With `never`, create it
yourself, for example in a Flyway or Liquibase migration, from the schema file for your database in the
`actor-jdbc` jar: `io/github/seonwkim/actor/jdbc/schema-{h2,postgresql,mysql,mariadb}.sql`.

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS actor_peer (
    service_name VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    node_id VARCHAR(500) NOT NULL,
    host VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    port INT NOT NULL,
    last_seen TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (service_name, node_id)
);
```

A node that crashes leaves its row behind; it is ignored once it is older than the ttl, and you can delete
old rows at any time.

### Redis

```yaml
spring:
  data:
    redis:
      host: redis
  actor:
    name: orders
    provider: cluster
    cluster:
      join: discovery
      discovery:
        method: redis
```

Each node is a hash under `actor:peer:<service>:<node address>` that expires after the ttl, so a crashed
node's entry removes itself. The starter reads the keys with `SCAN`, which sees one server: use a single
Redis or a primary with replicas (Sentinel), not Redis Cluster.

### Your own store

Implement `io.github.seonwkim.actor.spi.PeerRegistry` (in `actor-api`, no Pekko types) and declare it as a
bean. Set `discovery.method: custom`. A `PeerRegistry` bean of your own also replaces the `jdbc` and `redis`
stores.

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Bean
    PeerRegistry peerRegistry(MyStore store) {
        return new PeerRegistry() {
            public void register(Peer peer) { store.upsert(peer); }       // also marks it seen now
            public void deregister(Peer peer) { store.delete(peer); }
            public List<Peer> peers(String service, Duration ttl) { return store.seenWithin(service, ttl); }
        };
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @Bean
    fun peerRegistry(store: MyStore): PeerRegistry = object : PeerRegistry {
        override fun register(peer: Peer) = store.upsert(peer)            // also marks it seen now
        override fun deregister(peer: Peer) = store.delete(peer)
        override fun peers(service: String, ttl: Duration): List<Peer> = store.seenWithin(service, ttl)
    }
    ```

`MyStore` stands for your own storage code. A `Peer` is the service name, the node id, and the management
host and port. `heartbeat(peer)` runs every `heartbeat-interval` and calls `register` unless you override it.

Methods may block: the starter calls them on the blocking dispatcher. The starter owns the timers and the
shutdown hook; a store only stores and reads entries. Run `PeerRegistryContract` from `actor-test` against
your store to check it behaves like the built-in ones (see [Testing](../testing.md#contract-suites-for-your-own-store)).

## Other discovery methods

`discovery.method` also accepts Pekko's own methods. Each needs its library and its Pekko settings:

| `method` | Pekko method | Library |
|---|---|---|
| `kubernetes-api` | `kubernetes-api` | `pekko-discovery-kubernetes-api_3` (the pods' service account needs RBAC to list pods) |
| `dns` | `pekko-dns` | built in |
| `config` | `config` | built in; peers under `spring.actor.pekko.discovery.config.services` |

## Properties

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `spring.actor.cluster.join` | `seed-nodes` | `seed-nodes` or `discovery` |
| `spring.actor.cluster.seed-nodes` | none | Addresses to join, as `pekko://<name>@<host>:<port>` |
| `spring.actor.cluster.discovery.method` | none | `jdbc`, `redis`, `custom`, `kubernetes-api`, `dns` or `config` |
| `spring.actor.cluster.discovery.heartbeat-interval` | `5s` | How often a node renews its entry |
| `spring.actor.cluster.discovery.ttl` | `30s` | Entries older than this are ignored |
| `spring.actor.cluster.join-self` | `false` | Form a one-node cluster without seed nodes, for local runs and tests |
| `spring.actor.cluster.roles` | none | Roles of this node, for [sharded actors](sharded-actors.md#run-entities-on-some-nodes-only) and [singletons](singletons.md#limit-it-to-some-nodes) |
| `spring.actor.jdbc.initialize-schema` | `embedded` | When to create `actor_peer` and `actor_lease`: `embedded`, `always`, `never` |

## What the nodes need

- **Management port** (Pekko's default `7626`, `spring.actor.pekko.management.http.port`): Bootstrap contacts
  peers there. `spring.actor.pekko.management.http.hostname` must be an address other nodes can reach (the
  default is the machine's address). With `jdbc` or `redis` discovery the port may be `0`: the node registers
  the port it bound.
- **Remoting port** (`spring.actor.remote.port`, default `25520`) between all nodes.
- **The store** (database or Redis) from every node.
- The nodes of one cluster use the same `spring.actor.name`: it is the service name their entries are stored
  under.

The Kubernetes example has ready-made overlays for both stores, with the NetworkPolicies:
see `example/kubernetes/overlays/discovery-jdbc` and `discovery-redis` and the "Without RBAC" section of
its README.

Bootstrap waits for `pekko.management.cluster.bootstrap.contact-point-discovery.required-contact-point-nr`
(default `2`) peers before it forms a new cluster. Set it to `1` for a single replica.

With `join: discovery`, the split brain resolver defaults to `keep-majority`. To choose another strategy, or
to keep singletons and shards on one node with a lease, see [Split Brain and Leases](split-brain-and-leases.md).

## Securing the discovery store

With `jdbc` or `redis` discovery, the store decides which hosts a new node contacts and joins: Bootstrap
trusts every entry it reads. Leases in the same store ([Split Brain and Leases](split-brain-and-leases.md#leases))
decide which node may run a singleton or a shard, or stays up after a split. So whoever can write
`actor_peer`, `actor_lease` or the `actor:peer:` and `actor:lease:` keys can point new nodes at a host they
control, or take a lease. Treat the store as part of the cluster's trust boundary: only the nodes write to it.

Remoting (`25520`) accepts any connection unless you set up Pekko's TLS transport
(`spring.actor.pekko.remote.artery.transport: tls-tcp` and its `ssl` settings), and the management port
(`7626`) has no authentication. So the store's permissions and the network rules (only the cluster's nodes
reach these ports) are the controls.

**Redis.** Give the nodes a dedicated ACL user that can touch only the starter's keys and run only the
commands the stores use:

```text
ACL SETUSER actor-store on >change-me resetkeys ~actor:peer:* ~actor:lease:* resetchannels -@all +@connection +time +scan +hgetall +get +set +del +eval +evalsha +hset +pexpire
```

- `HSET`, `PEXPIRE`, `GET` and `DEL` also run inside the stores' Lua scripts, and Redis checks a script's
  commands against the same ACL.
- Turn on TLS (`spring.data.redis.ssl.enabled: true`) and auth (`spring.data.redis.username`, `password`).
- Don't share the Redis database with untrusted writers. `SCAN` lists key names of the whole database,
  whatever the user's key patterns.

**JDBC.** Give the nodes a database user with rights only on the two tables, and create the tables from your
migrations with another user (`spring.actor.jdbc.initialize-schema: never`):

```sql
-- PostgreSQL
CREATE ROLE actor_store LOGIN PASSWORD 'change-me';
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON actor_peer, actor_lease TO actor_store;

-- MySQL / MariaDB (orders is the schema)
CREATE USER 'actor_store'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'change-me';
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON orders.actor_peer TO 'actor_store'@'%';
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON orders.actor_lease TO 'actor_store'@'%';
```

No user that untrusted code can reach (another service, a reporting tool, an admin console) should be able to
write these tables.

The built-in stores use the application's `DataSource` and `RedisConnectionFactory`, so these rights are the
rights of the user the application connects as. If the application needs more rights on the same server,
give the stores their own connection: declare `PeerRegistry` and `LeaseStore` beans built on a separate
`DataSource` or `RedisConnectionFactory` (`new JdbcPeerRegistry(dataSource)`, `new JdbcLeaseStore(dataSource)`,
`new RedisPeerRegistry(connectionFactory, ttl)`, `new RedisLeaseStore(connectionFactory)`) and set
`discovery.method: custom` and `lease.store: custom` (see [Your own store](#your-own-store)).

## Related

- [Split Brain and Leases](split-brain-and-leases.md): what happens when nodes lose each other
- [Sharded Actors](sharded-actors.md) and [Cluster Singletons](singletons.md): what runs on the cluster
- [Kubernetes example](../../examples/kubernetes.md): discovery overlays and network policies
- [Testing](../testing.md#cluster-tests-with-actorcluster): several nodes in one JVM

<!-- Source: https://seonwkim.github.io/actor-spring-boot-starter/guides/cluster/split-brain-and-leases/ -->

# Split Brain and Leases

When nodes stop hearing from each other (a network split, a long GC pause, a crashed machine), each side
sees the other as unreachable. Without a decision, both sides keep running: a cluster singleton and a
sharded entity can then run twice, once on each side. A **downing strategy** (Pekko's split brain resolver)
decides which side stays and which side stops. A **lease** adds a lock in a store both sides can reach, so
only one side can hold it.

## Downing strategy

Set `spring.actor.cluster.downing.strategy`:

| `strategy` | Which side stays |
|---|---|
| `keep-majority` | The side with more nodes; on a tie, the side with the lowest address. |
| `lease-majority` | The side that takes the lease in `spring.actor.cluster.lease.store`. The bigger side tries first. |
| `static-quorum` | A side with at least `downing.quorum-size` nodes. Set it above half the cluster's size. |
| `keep-oldest` | The side with the oldest node. |
| `down-all` | No side: all nodes stop. |
| `none` | No downing. Unreachable nodes stay members until removed by hand. |

The default is `keep-majority` with `join: discovery`, and `none` otherwise. A cluster with no downing logs a
warning at startup. A node that is downed leaves the cluster and its actor system stops; with the default
`spring.actor.shutdown.exit-process: true`, the process exits too, and your platform (Kubernetes, systemd)
starts it again as a fresh node.

```yaml
spring:
  actor:
    provider: cluster
    cluster:
      downing:
        strategy: keep-majority
```

`keep-majority` needs no store, but on an even split (2 and 2) only the lowest address decides. When the
store is reachable from both sides, `lease-majority` decides by who takes the lease instead.

## Leases

A lease is a lock with an owner and an expiry, kept in a store. The holder renews it; when it stops renewing,
another node can take it after the lease's ttl. Three things can use one:

| Setting | Lease | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `downing.strategy: lease-majority` | one per cluster | Only the side that takes it stays up. |
| `singleton.use-lease: true` | one per cluster singleton | A singleton starts only after it takes its lease, so it never runs on two nodes. See [Cluster Singletons](singletons.md#leases-never-two-at-once). |
| `sharding.use-lease: true` | one per shard | A shard starts its entities only after it takes its lease. |

Each needs `spring.actor.cluster.lease.store`:

| `store` | Where leases live | Module |
|---|---|---|
| `jdbc` | The `actor_lease` table on the application's `DataSource` | `actor-jdbc` |
| `redis` | Keys with a TTL on the application's `RedisConnectionFactory` | `actor-redis` |
| `custom` | Your `LeaseStore` bean | none |

Whoever can write the lease store can take a lease, so the store is part of the cluster's trust boundary. See
[Securing the discovery store](cluster-formation.md#securing-the-discovery-store) for the Redis ACL and the
database grants.

```yaml
spring:
  actor:
    provider: cluster
    jdbc:
      initialize-schema: always   # creates actor_peer and actor_lease
    cluster:
      downing:
        strategy: lease-majority
      lease:
        store: jdbc
      singleton:
        use-lease: true
      sharding:
        use-lease: true
```

Timings:

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `lease.ttl` | `120s` | How long a lease stays held after its last renewal before another node may take it. |
| `lease.renew-interval` | `12s` | How often the holder renews it. Keep it well under the ttl. |
| `lease.expiry-margin` | `10s` | The holder treats the lease as lost this long before the ttl runs out, so it stops before another node can take over. Must be less than `ttl`. |

Times come from the store's clock (the database's `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`, Redis `TIME`). The holder also counts
the ttl on its own clock from the last successful renewal: if the store is unreachable until then (minus the
margin), it gives the lease up. A singleton or shard whose lease is lost stops.

Lease names: `<name>-pekko-sbr` for the downing lease, `<name>-singleton-<path>` for a singleton and
`<name>-shard-<type>-<shard id>` for a shard, where `<name>` is `spring.actor.name`. The owner is
`<name>@<host>:<port>` of the holding node.

### JDBC

`actor_lease` is created together with `actor_peer` when `spring.actor.jdbc.initialize-schema` is `always`
(or `embedded` with an embedded database). With `never`, create it from the schema file for your database in
the `actor-jdbc` jar: `io/github/seonwkim/actor/jdbc/schema-{h2,postgresql,mysql,mariadb}.sql`.

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS actor_lease (
    lease_name VARCHAR(500) NOT NULL,
    owner VARCHAR(500) NOT NULL,
    expires_at TIMESTAMP(3) NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (lease_name)
);
```

Taking a lease is one conditional `UPDATE` (free, expired or already ours), then an `INSERT` if no row exists.
The primary key makes only one of two concurrent inserts succeed.

### Redis

A lease is a key `actor:lease:<name>` set with `SET NX PX`; renew and release check the owner first. Redis
replicates to replicas asynchronously: if the primary fails right after a node took a lease, the new primary
may not have the key, and a second node can take it. Use the JDBC store, or a Redis without failover, when a
singleton must never run twice.

### Your own store

Implement `io.github.seonwkim.actor.spi.LeaseStore` (in `actor-api`, no Pekko types), declare it as a bean
and set `lease.store: custom`. A `LeaseStore` bean of your own also replaces the `jdbc` and `redis` stores.

The interface:

```java
public interface LeaseStore {
    boolean tryAcquire(String lease, String owner, Duration ttl); // free, expired or already ours
    boolean renew(String lease, String owner, Duration ttl);      // only while we hold it
    void release(String lease, String owner);                     // only if we hold it
    Optional<String> holder(String lease);                        // the current, unexpired owner
}
```

An implementation, as a bean:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Component
    public class MyLeaseStore implements LeaseStore {

        private final MyLeaseTable table; // your own storage code

        public MyLeaseStore(MyLeaseTable table) {
            this.table = table;
        }

        @Override
        public boolean tryAcquire(String lease, String owner, Duration ttl) {
            return table.insertOrTakeOver(lease, owner, ttl); // one atomic statement
        }

        @Override
        public boolean renew(String lease, String owner, Duration ttl) {
            return table.extendIfOwner(lease, owner, ttl);
        }

        @Override
        public void release(String lease, String owner) {
            table.deleteIfOwner(lease, owner);
        }

        @Override
        public Optional<String> holder(String lease) {
            return table.unexpiredOwner(lease);
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @Component
    class MyLeaseStore(private val table: MyLeaseTable) : LeaseStore { // MyLeaseTable: your own storage code

        override fun tryAcquire(lease: String, owner: String, ttl: Duration): Boolean =
            table.insertOrTakeOver(lease, owner, ttl) // one atomic statement

        override fun renew(lease: String, owner: String, ttl: Duration): Boolean =
            table.extendIfOwner(lease, owner, ttl)

        override fun release(lease: String, owner: String) =
            table.deleteIfOwner(lease, owner)

        override fun holder(lease: String): Optional<String> =
            table.unexpiredOwner(lease)
    }
    ```

`Duration` is `java.time.Duration` in both.

Each method must be atomic in the store. Methods may block: the starter calls them on the blocking
dispatcher, and owns the renewal timers. Run `LeaseStoreContract` from `actor-test` against your store to
check it (see [Testing](../testing.md#contract-suites-for-your-own-store)).

## Related

- [Cluster Singletons](singletons.md): what a singleton lease protects
- [Sharded Actors](sharded-actors.md): what a shard lease protects
- [Cluster Formation](cluster-formation.md): `actor-jdbc` and `actor-redis` also find peers
- [Production](../operations/production.md): graceful shutdown, so a leaving node is never downed

---

<!-- Source: https://seonwkim.github.io/actor-spring-boot-starter/guides/cluster/replicated-data/ -->

# Replicated Data

Replicated data is a map, a counter or a set that every node of the cluster keeps a copy of. Any node
reads and writes its own copy without a round trip, and the copies converge: changes made on different
nodes at the same time are merged, never lost. These are Pekko Distributed Data's CRDTs (conflict-free
replicated data types) behind a small API with no Pekko types.

Use it for small, shared, often-read state: feature flags, who is online, rate-limit counters, a cache of
settings. It is not a database: the data lives in memory and is gone when every node stops.

## Setup

Replicated data needs the cluster starter and cluster mode:

```yaml
spring:
  actor:
    provider: cluster
```

The starter then provides a `ReplicatedData` bean. Each node starts Pekko's replicator when its actor
system starts.

## Maps, counters and sets

`ReplicatedData` hands out a handle per name. Declare the handles you use as beans and inject them where
you need them:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Configuration
    class ReplicatedDataConfig {

        @Bean
        ReplicatedMap<String, Cart> carts(ReplicatedData data) {
            return data.map("carts");
        }

        @Bean
        ReplicatedCounter visits(ReplicatedData data) {
            return data.counter("visits");
        }

        @Bean
        ReplicatedSet<String> onlineUsers(ReplicatedData data) {
            return data.set("online-users");
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @Configuration
    class ReplicatedDataConfig {

        @Bean
        fun carts(data: ReplicatedData): ReplicatedMap<String, Cart> = data.map("carts")

        @Bean
        fun visits(data: ReplicatedData): ReplicatedCounter = data.counter("visits")

        @Bean
        fun onlineUsers(data: ReplicatedData): ReplicatedSet<String> = data.set("online-users")
    }
    ```

Or inject `ReplicatedData` and ask for a handle when the name is only known at run time, such as one
counter per tenant: `data.counter("requests-" + tenantId)`. A handle is a cheap view: two handles with the
same name and kind read and write the same data. Use each name for one kind only.

Every read and write returns a `CompletionStage`:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Service
    class CartService {
        private final ReplicatedMap<String, Cart> carts;

        CartService(ReplicatedMap<String, Cart> carts) {
            this.carts = carts;
        }

        CompletionStage<Void> save(String user, Cart cart) {
            return carts.put(user, cart);
        }

        CompletionStage<Optional<Cart>> find(String user) {
            return carts.get(user);
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @Service
    class CartService(private val carts: ReplicatedMap<String, Cart>) {

        // await() is kotlinx.coroutines.future.await (kotlinx-coroutines-core, which actor-kotlin brings)
        suspend fun save(user: String, cart: Cart) {
            carts.put(user, cart).await()
        }

        suspend fun find(user: String): Cart? = carts.get(user).await().orElse(null)
    }
    ```

| Type | Reads | Writes | When two nodes write at once |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ReplicatedMap<K, V>` | `entries()`, `get(key)` | `put(key, value)`, `remove(key)` | The later write to a key wins, by wall clock |
| `ReplicatedCounter` | `value()` | `increment(delta)`, `decrement(delta)` | Both changes count |
| `ReplicatedSet<E>` | `elements()` | `add(element)`, `remove(element)` | An add wins over a concurrent remove |

A map, counter or set nobody has written yet reads as empty (or zero).

## Consistency

Each read and write takes an optional `Consistency`: how many nodes to wait for.

| `Consistency` | Waits for | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| `local()` (default) | This node only | Fast reads and writes; other nodes see the change shortly after, in the background |
| `majority(timeout)` | More than half of the nodes | A write followed by a read on another node must see it |
| `all(timeout)` | Every node | Rarely: one unreachable node makes it fail |

=== "Java"

    ```java
    Consistency majority = Consistency.majority(Duration.ofSeconds(3));

    carts.put("alice", cart, majority);   // on node A
    carts.get("alice", majority);         // on node B: sees the write
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    val majority = Consistency.majority(Duration.ofSeconds(3))

    carts.put("alice", cart, majority)   // on node A
    carts.get("alice", majority)         // on node B: sees the write
    ```

A majority write followed by a majority read always sees the write, because the two majorities share at
least one node. If the nodes don't answer within the timeout, the stage completes with
`ReplicationTimeoutException`. A write that times out is still applied on this node and spreads to the
others later; it is not rolled back.

## What can be stored

Keys, values and set elements travel between nodes, so they must be serializable: `String`, `Integer`,
`Long`, or a type that implements `JsonSerializable` or `CborSerializable`, the same as actor messages.
Values that implement `JsonSerializable` use your application's `ObjectMapper`.

=== "Java"

    ```java
    public record Cart(List<String> items, int quantity) implements JsonSerializable {}
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    data class Cart(val items: List<String>, val quantity: Int) : JsonSerializable
    ```

## Limits

- **Small data.** Each node holds every entry, a new node receives all of them, and a change can send a
  whole map or set to the other nodes. Keep each one to thousands of entries, not millions; split big
  data over several names.
- **In memory.** The data survives a node restart while other nodes keep it, and is lost when all nodes
  stop. Keep the source of truth in a database.
- **Clock skew.** A map decides concurrent writes to the same key by wall clock, so keep the nodes' clocks
  in sync (NTP).

## Tuning

Pekko's settings under `pekko.cluster.distributed-data` apply through the raw override, for example a
shorter gossip interval:

```yaml
spring:
  actor:
    pekko:
      cluster:
        distributed-data:
          gossip-interval: 1s
```

## Related

- [Pub/Sub Topics](../core/pub-sub-topics.md): send messages to every subscriber instead of sharing state
- [Sharded Actors](sharded-actors.md): one owner per key, for state that must not merge
- [Cluster Formation](cluster-formation.md): forming the cluster the data is replicated over

<!-- Source: https://seonwkim.github.io/actor-spring-boot-starter/guides/data/state-in-a-database/ -->

# State in a Database

An actor's fields live in memory. They are lost when the actor stops: after a restart of the
application, a deploy, a passivated or moved [sharded entity](../cluster/sharded-actors.md), or a
[singleton](../cluster/singletons.md) that moves to another node. To keep the state, store it in your
database with the tools you already use: Spring Data JPA, `JdbcTemplate`, R2DBC.

The pattern is simple: the actor **loads** its state when it starts and **saves** it in the message handler
that changes it. Actors are Spring beans, so repositories and services are injected into them like into
any other bean. No module of the starter is needed for this.

Use this when you need the latest state only. When the history of changes matters (an audit trail, read
models, replays), use [event sourcing](event-sourcing.md) instead.

## Setup

Add Spring Data and your database driver next to the starter:

=== "Gradle"

    ```kotlin
    implementation("io.github.seonwkim:actor-spring-boot-starter:$version")
    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-data-jpa")
    runtimeOnly("org.postgresql:postgresql")
    ```

=== "Maven"

    ```xml
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.postgresql</groupId>
        <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
        <scope>runtime</scope>
    </dependency>
    ```

Configure the `DataSource` as usual (`spring.datasource.*`). The samples below use an `Order` JPA entity and
this repository, from the
[persistence example](https://github.com/seonWKim/actor-spring-boot-starter/tree/main/example/persistence):

=== "Java"

    ```java
    public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, String> {
        Optional<Order> findByOrderId(String orderId);
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    interface OrderRepository : JpaRepository<Order, String> {
        fun findByOrderId(orderId: String): Optional<Order>
    }
    ```

## Load on start, save on change

The actor id is the key of the row. `withState` runs once when the actor starts: load the row there. Each
handler that changes the state saves it before it replies.

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Component
    public class OrderActor implements SpringActor<OrderActor.Command> {

        private final OrderRepository orderRepository;

        public OrderActor(OrderRepository orderRepository) {
            this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
        }

        public interface Command {}

        public static class CreateOrder extends AskCommand<OrderResponse> implements Command {
            public final String customerId;
            public final double amount;

            public CreateOrder(String customerId, double amount) {
                this.customerId = customerId;
                this.amount = amount;
            }
        }

        public static class GetOrder extends AskCommand<OrderResponse> implements Command {}

        public record OrderResponse(boolean success, Order order, String message) {}

        @Override
        public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
            String orderId = actorContext.actorId();
            return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                    .withState(ctx -> new OrderBehavior(
                            ctx, orderId, orderRepository, orderRepository.findByOrderId(orderId).orElse(null)))
                    .onMessage(CreateOrder.class, OrderBehavior::onCreate)
                    .onMessage(GetOrder.class, OrderBehavior::onGet)
                    .build();
        }

        private static class OrderBehavior {
            private final SpringBehaviorContext<Command> ctx;
            private final String orderId;
            private final OrderRepository repository;
            private Order current; // null until the order is created

            OrderBehavior(SpringBehaviorContext<Command> ctx, String orderId, OrderRepository repository, Order current) {
                this.ctx = ctx;
                this.orderId = orderId;
                this.repository = repository;
                this.current = current;
            }

            SpringActorBehavior<Command> onCreate(CreateOrder msg) {
                if (current != null) {
                    msg.reply(new OrderResponse(false, current, "Order already exists"));
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                }
                current = repository.save(new Order(orderId, msg.customerId, msg.amount));
                ctx.getLog().info("Order created: {}", orderId);
                msg.reply(new OrderResponse(true, current, "Order created"));
                return SpringActorBehavior.same();
            }

            SpringActorBehavior<Command> onGet(GetOrder msg) {
                msg.reply(current == null
                        ? new OrderResponse(false, null, "Order not found")
                        : new OrderResponse(true, current, "OK"));
                return SpringActorBehavior.same();
            }
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @Component
    class OrderActor(private val orderRepository: OrderRepository) : SpringActor<OrderActor.Command> {

        sealed interface Command

        class CreateOrder(val customerId: String, val amount: Double) : AskCommand<OrderResponse>(), Command

        class GetOrder : AskCommand<OrderResponse>(), Command

        data class OrderResponse(val success: Boolean, val order: Order?, val message: String)

        override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
            val orderId = actorContext.actorId()
            return actorBehavior<Command>(actorContext)
                .withState { ctx ->
                    OrderBehavior(ctx, orderId, orderRepository, orderRepository.findByOrderId(orderId).orElse(null))
                }
                .onMessage(CreateOrder::class.java) { state, msg -> state.onCreate(msg) }
                .onMessage(GetOrder::class.java) { state, msg -> state.onGet(msg) }
                .build()
        }

        class OrderBehavior(
            private val ctx: SpringBehaviorContext<Command>,
            private val orderId: String,
            private val repository: OrderRepository,
            private var current: Order?, // null until the order is created
        ) {
            fun onCreate(msg: CreateOrder): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
                if (current != null) {
                    msg.reply(OrderResponse(false, current, "Order already exists"))
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same()
                }
                current = repository.save(Order(orderId, msg.customerId, msg.amount))
                ctx.log.info("Order created: {}", orderId)
                msg.reply(OrderResponse(true, current, "Order created"))
                return SpringActorBehavior.same()
            }

            fun onGet(msg: GetOrder): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
                msg.reply(
                    current?.let { OrderResponse(true, it, "OK") }
                        ?: OrderResponse(false, null, "Order not found"),
                )
                return SpringActorBehavior.same()
            }
        }
    }
    ```

Because an actor handles one message at a time, the state and the row never see two changes at once.
The database is still the source of truth: the next time the actor starts, it reads what was saved.

!!! warning "Save before you reply"
    Reply only after the save has succeeded. If the save throws, the caller gets no success reply, and the
    actor's field and the row don't drift apart. Catch the exception and reply with an error when the
    caller should learn about it instead of waiting for its timeout.

## Run it on the blocking dispatcher

JPA and JDBC calls block their thread until the database answers. On the default dispatcher, which every
actor shares, a few slow queries can hold all its threads and stall unrelated actors. Spawn actors that
block on the **blocking dispatcher** with `withBlockingDispatcher()`:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @RestController
    @RequestMapping("/api/orders")
    public class OrderController {

        private final SpringActorSystem actorSystem;

        public OrderController(SpringActorSystem actorSystem) {
            this.actorSystem = actorSystem;
        }

        @PostMapping("/{orderId}")
        public CompletionStage<OrderActor.OrderResponse> createOrder(
                @PathVariable String orderId, @RequestParam String customerId, @RequestParam double amount) {
            return actorSystem
                    .actor(OrderActor.class)
                    .withId(orderId)
                    .withBlockingDispatcher()
                    .getOrSpawn() // the running actor, or a new one on the blocking dispatcher
                    .thenCompose(order -> order.ask(new OrderActor.CreateOrder(customerId, amount))
                            .withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
                            .execute());
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @RestController
    @RequestMapping("/api/orders")
    class OrderController(private val actorSystem: SpringActorSystem) {

        // A suspend handler: see the Kotlin guide for what it needs on the classpath
        @PostMapping("/{orderId}")
        suspend fun createOrder(
            @PathVariable orderId: String,
            @RequestParam customerId: String,
            @RequestParam amount: Double,
        ): OrderActor.OrderResponse =
            actorSystem
                .actor<OrderActor, _>()
                .withId(orderId)
                .withBlockingDispatcher()
                .awaitGetOrSpawn() // the running actor, or a new one on the blocking dispatcher
                .awaitAsk(OrderActor.CreateOrder(customerId, amount), timeout = 5.seconds)
    }
    ```

Use `getOrSpawn()` on the spawn builder, as above, rather than `actorSystem.getOrSpawn(OrderActor.class, id)`:
only the builder carries the dispatcher.

The blocking dispatcher is Pekko's default blocking dispatcher, a fixed pool of threads. To run it on
virtual threads instead, set `spring.actor.virtual-threads.enabled: true` (or keep the default `auto` and
turn on Spring Boot's `spring.threads.virtual.enabled`). See [Dispatchers](../core/dispatchers.md).

## Non-blocking calls with R2DBC

Spring Data R2DBC returns a `Mono` instead of blocking, so the actor can stay on the default dispatcher.
Turn the result into a message with `pipeToSelf`: the actor handles it like any other message, one at a
time, so its state stays safe without locks.

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Component
    public class ReactiveOrderActor implements SpringActor<ReactiveOrderActor.Command> {

        private final ReactiveOrderRepository repository; // a Spring Data R2DBC repository

        public ReactiveOrderActor(ReactiveOrderRepository repository) {
            this.repository = repository;
        }

        public interface Command {}

        public record SaveOrder(Order order) implements Command {}

        // The result of a save, sent by the actor to itself.
        private record SaveDone(Order saved, Throwable failure) implements Command {}

        @Override
        public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
            return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                    .withState(ReactiveBehavior::new)
                    .onMessage(SaveOrder.class, ReactiveBehavior::onSave)
                    .onMessage(SaveDone.class, ReactiveBehavior::onSaveDone)
                    .build();
        }

        private class ReactiveBehavior {
            private final SpringBehaviorContext<Command> ctx;
            private Order current;

            ReactiveBehavior(SpringBehaviorContext<Command> ctx) {
                this.ctx = ctx;
            }

            SpringActorBehavior<Command> onSave(SaveOrder msg) {
                // Returns at once; the save runs on R2DBC's threads, not the actor's.
                ctx.pipeToSelf(repository.save(msg.order()).toFuture(), SaveDone::new);
                return SpringActorBehavior.same();
            }

            SpringActorBehavior<Command> onSaveDone(SaveDone done) {
                if (done.failure() != null) {
                    ctx.getLog().error("Save failed", done.failure());
                } else {
                    current = done.saved(); // state changes only inside a message handler
                }
                return SpringActorBehavior.same();
            }
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @Component
    class ReactiveOrderActor(
        private val repository: ReactiveOrderRepository, // a Spring Data R2DBC repository
    ) : SpringActor<ReactiveOrderActor.Command> {

        sealed interface Command

        data class SaveOrder(val order: Order) : Command

        // The result of a save, sent by the actor to itself.
        private data class SaveDone(val saved: Order?, val failure: Throwable?) : Command

        override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
            actorBehavior<Command>(actorContext)
                .withState { ctx -> ReactiveBehavior(ctx) }
                .onMessage(SaveOrder::class.java) { state, msg -> state.onSave(msg) }
                .onMessage(SaveDone::class.java) { state, done -> state.onSaveDone(done) }
                .build()

        private inner class ReactiveBehavior(private val ctx: SpringBehaviorContext<Command>) {
            private var current: Order? = null

            fun onSave(msg: SaveOrder): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
                // Returns at once; the save runs on R2DBC's threads, not the actor's.
                ctx.pipeToSelf(repository.save(msg.order).toFuture()) { saved, failure -> SaveDone(saved, failure) }
                return SpringActorBehavior.same()
            }

            fun onSaveDone(done: SaveDone): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
                if (done.failure != null) {
                    ctx.log.error("Save failed", done.failure)
                } else {
                    current = done.saved // state changes only inside a message handler
                }
                return SpringActorBehavior.same()
            }
        }
    }
    ```

To reply to the caller once the save is done, carry the `AskCommand` in the result message and call
`reply` in its handler.

!!! warning "Don't touch state in a callback"
    Never change actor state in `subscribe(...)`, `thenAccept(...)` or any other callback: it runs on
    another thread, alongside the actor. Send the result to the actor with `pipeToSelf` and change state
    in the handler.

## Transactions

When one change writes several tables, put the writes in a `@Transactional` method of a Spring service and
call it from the actor. Spring's transaction works as anywhere else, because the call runs on the actor's
thread from start to end.

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Service
    public class OrderService {

        private final OrderRepository orders;
        private final OrderItemRepository items;

        public OrderService(OrderRepository orders, OrderItemRepository items) {
            this.orders = orders;
            this.items = items;
        }

        @Transactional
        public Order createWithItems(String orderId, String customerId, double amount, List<OrderItem> newItems) {
            Order order = orders.save(new Order(orderId, customerId, amount));
            for (OrderItem item : newItems) {
                item.setOrder(order);
                items.save(item);
            }
            return order;
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @Service
    class OrderService(
        private val orders: OrderRepository,
        private val items: OrderItemRepository,
    ) {
        @Transactional
        fun createWithItems(orderId: String, customerId: String, amount: Double, newItems: List<OrderItem>): Order {
            val order = orders.save(Order(orderId, customerId, amount))
            for (item in newItems) {
                item.setOrder(order)
                items.save(item)
            }
            return order
        }
    }
    ```

Inject `OrderService` into the actor instead of the repositories, and call it in the handler. Run the actor
on the blocking dispatcher, as above. Don't put `@Transactional` on the actor class: the actor's handlers
are not called through a Spring proxy.

## Snapshots of large state

When building the state from many rows is slow, store a snapshot of it now and then: serialize the state
to JSON in a snapshot table every N changes or every few seconds, and on start, load the latest snapshot
before falling back to the rows. The persistence example's
[`SnapshotOrderActor`](https://github.com/seonWKim/actor-spring-boot-starter/tree/main/example/persistence/src/main/java/io/github/seonwkim/example/persistence/snapshot)
does this with its own `SnapshotStrategy` and `HybridSnapshotStrategy` classes. These classes belong to the
example, not to the starter.

[Event-sourced actors](event-sourcing.md) have snapshots built in (`snapshotEvery(n)`).

## Choosing an approach

| Approach | Use it when | What to watch |
|---|---|---|
| JPA or JDBC on the blocking dispatcher | The app already uses JPA, as most Spring apps do | Each call holds a thread of the blocking dispatcher. Size the pool, or use virtual threads |
| R2DBC with `pipeToSelf` | Many actors talk to the database at once, or the app is already reactive | Every result comes back as a message, so each call needs a result message type |
| Event sourcing with `actor-persistence` | The history of changes matters, not only the latest state | Events are a stored contract: their JSON shape must stay readable. See [Event-Sourced Actors](event-sourcing.md) |

## One writer per row

The pattern is safe because one actor owns one row. Keep it that way:

- **One node.** A regular actor with a given id runs once per node, so one node never has two writers.
- **Several nodes.** Each node can spawn its own `OrderActor` with the same id, and then two actors write
  the same row. Make the actor a [sharded entity](../cluster/sharded-actors.md) (one per id in the cluster)
  or, for a single global actor, a [singleton](../cluster/singletons.md). For extra safety, add a version
  column (`@Version` in JPA) so a stale write fails instead of overwriting.

## Pitfalls

- **Blocking on the default dispatcher.** Always spawn JPA and JDBC actors with `withBlockingDispatcher()`.
- **Changing state in callbacks.** Use `pipeToSelf`.
- **Replying before saving.** The caller then sees a success that may not be stored.
- **Lazy JPA associations.** The actor keeps the entity after the transaction has ended; load what you need
  in the query (`JOIN FETCH`) or map it to your own class.

## Related

- [Persistence example](../../examples/persistence.md): JPA, a hand-made event log and snapshots
