# Deployments

This guide covers how to release a new version of a clustered actor application without failing requests:
rolling updates, canary releases and blue-green switches, and how to change messages so that two versions
can run side by side.

The commands come from the [Kubernetes example](../../examples/kubernetes.md)
([`example/kubernetes`](https://github.com/seonWKim/actor-spring-boot-starter/tree/main/example/kubernetes)),
which runs the chat example as a three-pod cluster on a local kind cluster. The ideas apply to any platform.

## Choosing a strategy

| Strategy | What runs | Traffic | Versions mix in one cluster | Script |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rolling update | One cluster; old and new pods side by side during the rollout | Moves pod by pod | Yes | `kubectl set image` |
| Canary | One cluster; a few new pods join the running cluster | Share = canary pods / all pods | Yes | `scripts/canary.sh` |
| Blue-green | Two separate clusters (blue and green) | Switches in one step | No | `scripts/blue-green.sh` |

- Use a **rolling update** for most releases. It needs no extra capacity beyond one pod.
- Use a **canary** when you want a few real requests on the new version first, with a quick way back.
- Use **blue-green** when the new version cannot talk to the old one (an incompatible message change) or
  when you want to switch all traffic at once. It needs twice the pods for a while, and in-memory state
  does not move.

All three rely on the [graceful shutdown](production.md#graceful-shutdown) settings: each old pod leaves the
cluster on purpose, so its sharded entities and singletons move instead of waiting for the split brain
resolver.

## Rolling update

A rolling update replaces pods one at a time inside one cluster. The example's Deployment adds a new pod
before it removes an old one, so the cluster never drops below its size:

```yaml
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 0    # never fewer than 3 ready pods
      maxSurge: 1          # start one new pod before stopping an old one
```

Each new pod joins the running cluster. Its readiness probe includes `actorCluster`, so it gets traffic only
once it is an `Up` member (see [Health checks](production.md#health-checks)). Then Kubernetes stops an old
pod: the `preStop` sleep lets the load balancer drop it, and coordinated shutdown moves its entities to the
other nodes.

```bash
kubectl set image deployment/spring-actor spring-actor=spring-actor-chat:v2 -n spring-actor
kubectl rollout status deployment/spring-actor -n spring-actor

# Go back to the previous version
kubectl rollout undo deployment/spring-actor -n spring-actor
```

## Canary

A canary runs a few pods of the new version in the same cluster as the main pods. `canary.sh start` copies
the live Deployment as `spring-actor-canary` with the new image and a `track: canary` label. The Services
select `app=spring-actor`, so they send the canary pods their share of the requests: with three main pods and
one canary, about one in four.

```bash
cd example/kubernetes
scripts/canary.sh start spring-actor-chat:v3      # one canary pod; `start <image> 2` for two
scripts/canary.sh promote                         # roll the main pods to v3, then remove the canary
# scripts/canary.sh abort                         # or remove the canary and keep the main pods as they are
```

Because the canary is a member of the same cluster, sharded entities can move to it and it exchanges messages
with the old pods. Both versions must read each other's messages and entity state (see
[Message compatibility](#message-compatibility-across-versions)).

## Blue-green

Blue-green starts the new version as a second, separate cluster. `blue-green.sh deploy` copies the live
Deployment as `spring-actor-green` with the new image, labels its pods `app=spring-actor-green`, and points
its Kubernetes API discovery at that label
(`--spring.actor.pekko.discovery.kubernetes-api.pod-label-selector=app=spring-actor-green`). So green forms
its own cluster and never exchanges messages with blue.

Before green starts, `deploy` also copies each NetworkPolicy that selects `app=spring-actor` (for example
`spring-actor-green` from `spring-actor`, and `spring-actor-green-store` from `spring-actor-store` in the
discovery overlays), with every `app=spring-actor` selector changed to `app=spring-actor-green`. Green gets
the same restrictions as blue, and remoting (25520) and management (7626) open only between pods of the same
color: blue and green cannot reach each other's cluster ports. A canary keeps `app=spring-actor`, so blue's
policies cover it.

### The release pipeline

A blue-green release runs in four stages. Each one waits for a signal before the next starts:

| Stage | Command | Waits for |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Warm up | `blue-green.sh deploy <image>` | every green pod answers `UP` on `/actuator/health/warmup`, then is ready |
| 2. Activate | `blue-green.sh activate` | the [generation endpoint](#the-active-generation) accepts green; then the HTTP Service's selector picks the green pods |
| 3. Verify | `blue-green.sh verify` | the generation record says green, and the Service's ready endpoints are exactly the green pods |
| 4. Retire | `blue-green.sh retire` | run it once green has served for a while; it deletes blue |

```bash
cd example/kubernetes
scripts/blue-green.sh deploy spring-actor-chat:v4   # start green beside blue and wait until it is warm
scripts/blue-green.sh activate                      # green becomes the active generation; the Service selects it
scripts/blue-green.sh verify                        # wait until only green pods serve
# scripts/blue-green.sh rollback                    # activate blue again (a new epoch) and select it
scripts/blue-green.sh retire                        # delete blue
```

The first stage gates on **warm-up**, not on `kubectl rollout status` or the Deployment's `Available`
condition. Those follow traffic readiness, and in a pipeline where the standby color refuses traffic until it
is activated they never come. The warm-up group says only that the pod can be activated:

- the pod is an `Up` member of its cluster,
- the cluster has at least `management.health.actor.warmup.min-members` `Up` members (the example sets 2),
- and the discovery store answers, when the cluster forms through `jdbc` or `redis` discovery.

It never depends on which color is active. The three probes stay apart: liveness says whether to restart the
pod, readiness whether to send it traffic, and warm-up whether it can be activated (see
[Health checks](production.md#warm-up)).

In-memory state does not move: entities, singletons and topics start empty on green. Keep state that must
survive the switch in a database or event journal both clusters read
([State in a Database](../data/state-in-a-database.md), [Event-Sourced Actors](../data/event-sourcing.md)).
Until `retire`, `rollback` sends traffic back to blue, which still has its state.

### The active generation

Which color is active is a record in the store the cluster already uses (Redis or the database), not only a
Service selector. Each record is a **generation**: a color, an **epoch** that grows by one with every
activation, the deployment operation ID that activated it, and when. The application can read it, and the
pipeline changes it only through a compare-and-set:

- **Competing deploys fail loudly.** An activation names the epoch it expects to be active. If another deploy
  activated in between, it is rejected (`EPOCH_MISMATCH`, HTTP 409) and nothing changes. Of several
  activations that expect the same epoch, exactly one wins.
- **Retries are idempotent.** An activation carries an operation ID. Retrying it with the same color and
  expected epoch returns the generation it activated the first time (`ALREADY_ACTIVATED`, HTTP 200), even
  after the epoch has moved on. The same operation ID with another color or epoch is `OPERATION_CONFLICT`
  (409). A pipeline keeps the expected epoch and the operation ID it used, and sends both again when it
  retries.
- **Old work stays fenced.** Blue, then green, then blue again gives epochs 1, 2 and 3. Work that blue stamped
  in its first turn carries epoch 1 and is refused in its second (epoch 3), because the epoch never goes back.

Turn it on in each color with its color and a store:

```yaml
spring:
  actor:
    generation:
      color: blue          # green in the other deployment
      store: redis         # jdbc: the actor_generation table; custom: your GenerationStore bean
      # name: orders       # the record both colors share; default: spring.actor.name
      # refresh: 1s        # how long a node reuses a read of the record
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,generation
  endpoint:
    generation:
      access: unrestricted   # activation is a write: read-only by default
```

**The `generation` endpoint.** `GET /actuator/generation` returns this node's color and the active
generation. `POST /actuator/generation` with `color`, `expectedEpoch` (0 before the first activation) and
`operationId` activates a color:

```bash
curl -u deployer:$PASSWORD -X POST localhost:8080/actuator/generation \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"color":"green","expectedEpoch":1,"operationId":"release-2026-11-11-1"}'
# {"outcome":"ACTIVATED","generation":{"color":"green","epoch":2,"operationId":"release-2026-11-11-1",...}}
```

Activation needs an authenticated user: a request without one is answered `401` (`UNAUTHENTICATED`). Secure
the endpoint with Spring Security like any other write endpoint, for example with a role:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain actuator(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http.securityMatcher(EndpointRequest.to("generation"))
                .authorizeHttpRequests(requests -> requests
                        .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST).hasRole("DEPLOYER")
                        .anyRequest().permitAll())
                .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
                .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable()) // called by a pipeline, not a browser session
                .build();
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @Bean
    fun actuator(http: HttpSecurity): SecurityFilterChain =
        http.securityMatcher(EndpointRequest.to("generation"))
            .authorizeHttpRequests {
                it.requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST).hasRole("DEPLOYER")
                    .anyRequest().permitAll()
            }
            .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
            .csrf { it.disable() } // called by a pipeline, not a browser session
            .build()
    ```

**Audit.** Every attempt that reaches the endpoint, or `DeploymentGeneration.activate` in your code, publishes
an `ActivationEvent` (an `ApplicationEvent`) with the requested color, expected epoch, operation ID, the
user's name and the result. The starter also logs it (`INFO` when accepted, `WARN` when rejected) and counts
it in `actor.generation.activations`, tagged with `outcome`. A request that Spring Security turns away never
reaches the endpoint, so it shows in Spring Security's events instead.

**Fencing in your code.** Inject `DeploymentGeneration`. Stamp work with `stamp()` where it starts (it
fails when this node's color is not active), and `check(epoch)` it where it runs. A stale epoch throws
`StaleGenerationException`, the retryable outcome of [reliable delivery](../core/reliable-delivery.md#stale-generation-not-the-owner-yet-or-anymore):

=== "Java"

    ```java
    long epoch = generation.stamp();                       // where the work starts
    sender.send(new ChargeOrder(orderId, epoch), key);

    .onMessage(ChargeOrder.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
        generation.check(msg.epoch());                     // StaleGenerationException if it is old
        payments.charge(msg.orderId());
        return SpringActorBehavior.same();
    })
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    val epoch = generation.stamp()                         // where the work starts
    sender.send(ChargeOrder(orderId, epoch), key)

    .onMessage(ChargeOrder::class.java) { _, msg ->
        generation.check(msg.epoch)                        // StaleGenerationException if it is old
        payments.charge(msg.orderId)
        SpringActorBehavior.same()
    }
    ```

A node reuses a read of the record for `spring.actor.generation.refresh` (1 second), so for up to that long
after an activation elsewhere it still accepts the old epoch. Where that matters, keep the epoch with the
data and compare it in the write itself (`UPDATE ... WHERE epoch <= ?`).

**Stores.** `jdbc` keeps one row per activation in `actor_generation` (created with the other actor-jdbc
tables): the primary key on deployment and epoch is the compare-and-set. `redis` keeps the record and the
operation IDs in two hashes and changes them in one Lua script. Redis replicates asynchronously, so a failover
can lose an activation it had just accepted; use `jdbc` where that is not acceptable. Your own
`GenerationStore` bean replaces both, and must pass `GenerationStoreContract` from `actor-test`.

### Requests at the cutover

In the example the Service selector switches the colors, and readiness does not depend on the color. So
`deploy` waits for warm-up **and** then for the green pods to be ready. Warm-up alone is not enough there:
a pod can be warm before its readiness probe first passes (the example's probe starts after 30 seconds),
and a Service that selects only pods that are not ready yet has no endpoints. Measured on kind with
`test-strategies.sh` (four workers asking sharded entities):

| `deploy` waited for | Requests | Failed | Service served only green |
|---|---|---|---|
| warm-up only | 15,057 | 20, all within 10 seconds after `activate` | 15 seconds after `activate` |
| warm-up, then ready (the script today) | 23,151 and 22,890 (two runs) | 0 and 0 | at the first check after `activate` |

Blue keeps running and serving until `retire`, so a node whose proxy rules still point at blue for a moment
after the switch still gets answers.

When readiness itself switches the colors (the standby refuses traffic until it is activated, and one
Service selects both), the cutover waits for readiness to propagate: each pod's readiness probe has to pass
(`periodSeconds` times `successThreshold` for the new color, `periodSeconds` times `failureThreshold` for the
old one), then the endpoint controller and every node's kube-proxy update. **Shorter probe intervals shorten
that window but don't close it**: requests routed during it reach a pod that is about to leave or none at
all. This mode was not measured here. Close the window with draining instead:

- switch with the Service selector (or another routing change) while both colors are ready, and keep the old
  pods running until `verify` shows the Service no longer selects them (`retire` comes last);
- the `preStop` sleep (10 seconds in the example) keeps a terminating pod serving while the endpoint removal
  propagates;
- `server.shutdown: graceful` finishes the requests the pod has already accepted.

`scripts/test-strategies.sh` prints, for the blue-green step, how long the Service took to serve only green
and how many requests failed from activation on.

## Testing the strategies under load

`scripts/test-strategies.sh` runs all three strategies on the kind cluster from `setup-local.sh` while
`scripts/load.sh` sends requests, and fails if any request failed:

```bash
cd example/kubernetes
./setup-local.sh
scripts/test-strategies.sh
# rolling        total=... ok=... failed=0 ok
# canary         total=... ok=... failed=0 ok
# blue-green     total=... ok=... failed=0 ok
```

It runs, in order: a rolling update to `v2` (120 seconds of load), a canary of `v3` that is then promoted
(180 seconds), and a blue-green release of `v4` through the four stages above (90 seconds, then `retire`). Each step's load runs four workers that ask
sharded entities (`/hello?message=hi&entityId=e<0-49>`).

What it checks and what it does not:

- `load.sh` counts a request as ok only when the actor replied. The chat app answers `200` with
  `Request timed out ...` when an ask fails, so the HTTP status alone would hide lost messages.
- The new versions are retags of the same image, so it checks the rollout mechanics (joining, leaving,
  entities moving, the Service switching), not a change in the code.

## Message compatibility across versions

**Rolling updates and canaries mix versions in one cluster.** Old and new pods exchange messages, and a
sharded entity can move from an old pod to a new one. Every message and every piece of entity state that
crosses nodes must be readable by both versions:

- Add fields as optional. The old version must accept a message with the new field, and the new version a
  message without it.
- Don't rename or remove fields or message types in the same release.
- Keep each type on the same serializer (`JsonSerializable` or `CborSerializable`).
- Make an incompatible change in two releases: first one that reads both formats, then one that writes the
  new format.

For example, a second release adds an optional field to a command:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    // v1
    public static class SayHello extends AskCommand<String> implements Command {
        public final String message;

        public SayHello(String message) {
            this.message = message;
        }
    }

    // v2: a new, optional field. Messages from v1 nodes don't have it.
    public static class SayHello extends AskCommand<String> implements Command {
        public final String message;
        @Nullable public final String language;

        public SayHello(String message, @Nullable String language) {
            this.message = message;
            this.language = language;
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    // v1
    class SayHello(val message: String) : AskCommand<String>(), Command

    // v2: a new, optional field. Messages from v1 nodes don't have it.
    class SayHello(val message: String, val language: String? = null) : AskCommand<String>(), Command
    ```

The starter's build checks this on every change: `MixedVersionMessageTest` runs two nodes in one JVM,
one with a message class and one with the same class plus a field, and sends a message each way between
sharded entities. The old node reads the new message and ignores the field it doesn't know; the new node
reads the old message with the missing field as `null`. The test covers `JsonSerializable` messages with
the starter's default Jackson settings. It does not cover a
renamed or removed field, a renamed class, or stored events and snapshots. To run the same check on your own
messages, see [Two versions of a message in one cluster](../testing.md#two-versions-of-a-message-in-one-cluster).

On Kubernetes, this was also measured on kind with a canary of the chat app: adding a field to `SayHello` lost no requests
(28,842 of 28,842), while renaming the class lost 104 of 7,105, which timed out because the old nodes could
not read the new type.

**Blue-green never mixes versions.** The two clusters never exchange messages, so the message format can
change freely. Stored state is different: events and snapshots in a journal or database must still be
readable by the new version (see [Event-Sourced Actors](../data/event-sourcing.md)).

## Rollback

| Strategy | How to go back |
|---|---|
| Rolling update | `kubectl rollout undo deployment/spring-actor -n spring-actor`: a rolling update in the other direction, so the same compatibility rules apply |
| Canary | `scripts/canary.sh abort` removes the canary pods; the main pods were never changed |
| Blue-green | `scripts/blue-green.sh rollback` until `retire`; blue still has its in-memory state |

## Related

- [Running in Production](production.md): graceful shutdown, health checks and the production checklist
- [Monitoring](monitoring.md): watch `actor.cluster.members` and `actor.cluster.unreachable` during a rollout
- [Kubernetes example](../../examples/kubernetes.md): the manifests and scripts on this page
- [Sharded Actors](../cluster/sharded-actors.md)

# Configuration Reference

This page lists every configuration key the starter and its modules read, with its default and what it does.

The keys are published as Spring Boot configuration metadata
(`META-INF/spring-configuration-metadata.json` in the `actor-autoconfigure` and `actor-metrics` jars), so
IDEs offer completion and documentation for them in `application.yml` and `application.properties`.

There are three kinds of settings:

- **Typed keys** (`spring.actor.*`, `management.*`): bound to a properties class and checked at startup.
- **Raw Pekko keys** (any other key under `spring.actor.*`): passed to Pekko as they are.
- **Environment variables** (`ACTOR_METRICS_*`): read only by the optional metrics Java agent.

## Where the keys live

All typed keys are bound by three `@ConfigurationProperties` classes. The store and persistence modules
(`actor-jdbc`, `actor-redis`, `actor-persistence`, `actor-projection`) have no properties class of their
own: their keys are part of `ActorProperties`, and they take their connection from the application's
`DataSource` or `RedisConnectionFactory`.

| Class | Prefix | Module |
|---|---|---|
| `ActorProperties` | `spring.actor` | `actor-autoconfigure` (in every starter) |
| `PekkoManagementProperties` | `spring.actor.pekko.management` | `actor-autoconfigure` |
| `ActorMetricsProperties` | `spring.actor.metrics` | `actor-metrics` |

Typed keys are validated when the application starts. A bad value stops it with a message that names
the key, for example `spring.actor.remote.port must be between 0 and 65535, got 70000`.

## Actor system

| Key | Default | Sets Pekko key | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `spring.actor.enabled` | `true` | none | Whether the starter starts an actor system. `false` turns off every actor auto-configuration while the starter stays on the classpath. |
| `spring.actor.name` | `system` | `pekko.name` | Name of the actor system. Letters, digits, `-` and `_`, starting with a letter or digit. Nodes of one cluster must use the same name. |
| `spring.actor.provider` | `local` | `pekko.actor.provider` | How actors reach each other: `local` (one JVM), `remote` (reachable from other nodes, no cluster membership) or `cluster`. `remote` and `cluster` need `actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster`. |

## Remoting

Used with `provider: remote` or `provider: cluster`.

| Key | Default | Sets Pekko key | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `spring.actor.remote.hostname` | Pekko's default | `pekko.remote.artery.canonical.hostname` | Host name or address other nodes use to reach this node. |
| `spring.actor.remote.port` | Pekko's default (`25520`) | `pekko.remote.artery.canonical.port` | Port this node listens on for other nodes, `0` to `65535`. `0` picks a free port. |

## Cluster

Used with `provider: cluster`. See [Cluster Formation](../cluster/cluster-formation.md) and
[Split Brain and Leases](../cluster/split-brain-and-leases.md).

### Joining

| Key | Default | Sets Pekko key | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `spring.actor.cluster.join` | `seed-nodes` | none | How this node finds the cluster: `seed-nodes` (the listed nodes) or `discovery` (peers found through `discovery.method`, with Pekko Cluster Bootstrap). |
| `spring.actor.cluster.seed-nodes` | none | `pekko.cluster.seed-nodes` | Nodes to join at startup, as `pekko://<name>@<host>:<port>`. Not with `join: discovery`. |
| `spring.actor.cluster.join-self` | `false` | none | Joins this node to itself: a one-node cluster without seed nodes, also on port `0`. For local runs and tests. Not with `seed-nodes` or `join: discovery`. With Pekko Management on the classpath, Cluster Bootstrap is not started for this node. |
| `spring.actor.cluster.roles` | none | `pekko.cluster.roles` | Roles of this node. Sharded actors and singletons can be limited to a role. |

### Discovery

Used with `join: discovery`.

| Key | Default | Sets Pekko key | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `spring.actor.cluster.discovery.method` | none | `pekko.discovery.method` | Where peers are found: `jdbc` (needs `actor-jdbc`), `redis` (needs `actor-redis`), `custom` (your `PeerRegistry` bean), `kubernetes-api`, `dns` or `config`. Required with `join: discovery`. A `PeerRegistry` bean of your own replaces the `jdbc` and `redis` stores. |
| `spring.actor.cluster.discovery.heartbeat-interval` | `5s` | none | How often a node renews its own entry (`jdbc`, `redis`, `custom`). Must be positive. |
| `spring.actor.cluster.discovery.ttl` | `30s` | none | How long an entry counts as alive after its last renewal (`jdbc`, `redis`, `custom`). Must be positive. |

### Downing (split brain resolver)

| Key | Default | Sets Pekko key | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `spring.actor.cluster.downing.strategy` | `keep-majority` with `join: discovery`, else `none` | `pekko.cluster.downing-provider-class`, `pekko.cluster.split-brain-resolver.active-strategy` | Which side of a network split stays up: `keep-majority`, `lease-majority`, `static-quorum`, `keep-oldest`, `down-all` or `none`. A cluster without downing logs a warning. |
| `spring.actor.cluster.downing.quorum-size` | none | `pekko.cluster.split-brain-resolver.static-quorum.quorum-size` | Nodes a side needs to stay up. Required with `static-quorum`; at least `1`. Set it above half the cluster's size. |

### Leases

| Key | Default | Sets Pekko key | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `spring.actor.cluster.lease.store` | none | none | Where leases live: `jdbc` (needs `actor-jdbc`), `redis` (needs `actor-redis`) or `custom` (your `LeaseStore` bean). Required by `downing.strategy: lease-majority`, `singleton.use-lease` and `sharding.use-lease`. |
| `spring.actor.cluster.lease.ttl` | `120s` | `spring-actor.lease.heartbeat-timeout` | How long a lease stays held after its last renewal before another node may take it. |
| `spring.actor.cluster.lease.renew-interval` | `12s` | `spring-actor.lease.heartbeat-interval` | How often the holder renews a lease. |
| `spring.actor.cluster.lease.expiry-margin` | `10s` | `spring-actor.lease.expiry-margin` | The holder treats its lease as lost this long before the ttl ends, so it stops before another node can take the lease. Must be less than `ttl`. |
| `spring.actor.cluster.singleton.role` | none | `pekko.cluster.singleton.role` | Cluster singletons run only on nodes with this role. Set the same value on every node. |
| `spring.actor.cluster.singleton.use-lease` | `false` | `pekko.cluster.singleton.use-lease` | A cluster singleton runs only while it holds a lease, so two nodes never run it at once, even during a split. |
| `spring.actor.cluster.sharding.use-lease` | `false` | `pekko.cluster.sharding.use-lease` | Each shard runs only while it holds a lease. |

### Pekko Management

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `spring.actor.pekko.management.enabled` | `true` | Whether to start the Pekko Management HTTP server and Cluster Bootstrap in cluster mode, when the Pekko Management libraries are on the classpath. The server's own settings (`spring.actor.pekko.management.http.port`, ...) are raw Pekko keys. |

## Database tables

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `spring.actor.jdbc.initialize-schema` | `embedded` | When to create the `actor-jdbc` tables (`actor_peer`, `actor_lease`): `embedded` (only in an embedded database), `always`, or `never` (you create them from the `schema-*.sql` files in `actor-jdbc`). |
| `spring.actor.persistence.initialize-schema` | `embedded` | When to create the `actor-persistence` tables (`event_journal`, `event_tag`, `snapshot`) and the `actor-projection` offset tables: `embedded`, `always` or `never`. See [Event-Sourced Actors](../data/event-sourcing.md#tables) and [Projections](../data/projections.md). |

## Dispatchers and threads

See [Dispatchers](../core/dispatchers.md).

| Key | Default | Sets Pekko key | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `spring.actor.dispatchers.<name>.executor` | none | `<name>.*` | Declares a dispatcher that runs on the named Spring `Executor` bean (for example a `ThreadPoolTaskExecutor`). Actors pick it with `withDispatcherFromConfig("<name>")`. |
| `spring.actor.dispatchers.<name>.virtual` | `false` | `<name>.executor` | Declares a dispatcher that runs on virtual threads, one per task. Set either `executor` or `virtual: true`, not both. |
| `spring.actor.dispatchers.<name>.throughput` | Pekko's default (`5`) | `<name>.throughput` | Messages an actor processes before its thread moves to the next actor. At least `1`. |
| `spring.actor.virtual-threads.enabled` | `auto` | `pekko.actor.default-blocking-io-dispatcher.executor` | Runs the blocking dispatcher (`withBlockingDispatcher()`) on virtual threads: `auto`, `true` or `false`. `auto` follows `spring.threads.virtual.enabled`. The default dispatcher always stays on platform threads. |

A dispatcher name is letters, digits, `-` and `_`, and must not be `pekko` or the name of a typed key
(`name`, `cluster`, `dispatchers`, ...).

## Startup checks

See [What not to do in an actor bean](../core/actors.md#what-not-to-do-in-an-actor-bean).

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `spring.actor.validation.actor-beans` | `warn` | What happens when an actor bean has a mutable instance field (neither `static`, `final` nor injected) or is a Spring AOP proxy: `warn` logs each problem, `fail` stops startup, `off` skips the checks. |

## Reliable delivery

See [Reliable Delivery](../core/reliable-delivery.md). A receiver can override `idempotency-ttl` in code, and a sender its whole `RetryPolicy`.

| Key | Default | Sets Pekko key | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `spring.actor.delivery.idempotency-ttl` | `10m` | `spring-actor.delivery.idempotency-ttl` | How long a receiver remembers the idempotency key of a message it handled; a message with a remembered key is acknowledged again without running the handler. Must be positive. |
| `spring.actor.delivery.max-remembered-keys` | `10000` | `spring-actor.delivery.max-remembered-keys` | The most keys one receiver remembers; past it, the oldest are forgotten first. At least `1`. |
| `spring.actor.delivery.retry.max-attempts` | `5` | none | Attempts in total, including the first. |
| `spring.actor.delivery.retry.timeout` | `30s` | none | Time from the first attempt after which a sender gives up; no attempt starts after it. |
| `spring.actor.delivery.retry.attempt-timeout` | `3s` | none | How long one attempt waits for the ack. |
| `spring.actor.delivery.retry.initial-backoff` | `200ms` | none | The backoff before the second attempt; it doubles up to `max-backoff`, with full jitter. |
| `spring.actor.delivery.retry.max-backoff` | `5s` | none | The longest backoff between attempts. |

## Blue-green generation

See [The active generation](deployments.md#the-active-generation). Blue-green activation is on when
`color` is set.

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `spring.actor.generation.color` | none | This deployment's color, for example `blue` or `green`. Setting it turns on blue-green activation, `DeploymentGeneration` and the `generation` Actuator endpoint; each color runs with its own value. |
| `spring.actor.generation.store` | none | Where the active generation is kept: `jdbc` (the `actor_generation` table, needs `actor-jdbc`), `redis` (needs `actor-redis`) or `custom` (your `GenerationStore` bean). |
| `spring.actor.generation.name` | `spring.actor.name` | Name of the record both colors share in the store. |
| `spring.actor.generation.refresh` | `1s` | How long a read of the active generation is reused before the store is read again: the longest a node takes to see an activation made elsewhere. `0` reads the store every time. Must not be negative. |

## Shutdown

See [Graceful shutdown](production.md#graceful-shutdown).

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `spring.actor.shutdown.timeout` | `20s` | How long closing the Spring context waits for the actor system's coordinated shutdown. Must be positive. |
| `spring.actor.shutdown.exit-process` | `true` | When the actor system terminates by itself (for example after this node is downed), the context closes; with this set, the process then exits with status 1 so an orchestrator restarts it. |

## Metrics

Needs `actor-metrics` and a Micrometer `MeterRegistry`. See [Monitoring](monitoring.md).

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `spring.actor.metrics.enabled` | `true` | Whether to register the actor meters, the actor `MetricsRegistry` bean and, in cluster mode, the `actor.cluster.*` and `actor.sharding.*` meters. |
| `spring.actor.metrics.path-tag-limit` | `0` | How many actor paths get their own `actor.path` tag on the `actor.message.*` meters; the rest share `actor.path=other`. `0` adds no `actor.path` tag, so the series count never grows with the number of actors. |

## Actuator

Need Spring Boot Actuator. See [Health checks](production.md#health-checks) and
[The actors endpoint](monitoring.md#the-actors-endpoint).

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `management.health.actor.enabled` | `true` | Whether to add the `actorSystem` and (in cluster mode) `actorCluster` health components. |
| `management.endpoint.actors.access` | `unrestricted` | Access to the `actors` endpoint (cluster mode): `unrestricted`, `read-only` or `none`. `none` turns it off. Spring Boot adds this key for every endpoint. |
| `management.endpoint.actors.cache.time-to-live` | `0ms` | How long a response of the `actors` endpoint may be cached. Spring Boot adds this key for every endpoint. |

`management.endpoint.actors.enabled` also appears in the metadata. Spring Boot generates it for every
endpoint and marks it deprecated; use `access` instead.

## Spring Boot keys that matter

These are Spring Boot's own keys. The starter reads or depends on them:

| Key | Why |
|---|---|
| `spring.threads.virtual.enabled` | `spring.actor.virtual-threads.enabled: auto` follows it. |
| `server.shutdown: graceful` and `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase` | The web server drains requests before the actor system stops. See [Shutdown order](production.md#shutdown-order). |
| `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include` | The `actors` and `prometheus` endpoints are exposed over HTTP only when listed here. |
| `management.endpoint.health.group.readiness.include` | Add `actorCluster` to gate traffic on cluster membership. |

## Example

```yaml
spring:
  actor:
    name: orders
    provider: cluster
    remote:
      hostname: 10.0.0.7
      port: 25520
    cluster:
      seed-nodes:
        - pekko://orders@10.0.0.7:25520
        - pekko://orders@10.0.0.8:25520
      roles: api
      downing:
        strategy: keep-majority
    shutdown:
      timeout: 25s
```

## Raw Pekko keys (`spring.actor.*`)

Every other key under `spring.actor.*` is passed unchanged to the Pekko actor system configuration,
with the `spring.actor` prefix removed. For example, `spring.actor.pekko.loglevel` becomes
`pekko.loglevel`, and a dispatcher defined at `spring.actor.my-dispatcher` becomes `my-dispatcher`.
Comma-separated string values are turned into lists, and a single value for a key that Pekko reads as
a list is a one-item list: `spring.actor.pekko.cluster.seed-nodes=pekko://orders@10.0.0.7:25521` works
like `seed-nodes[0]`. See the
[Pekko reference configuration](https://pekko.apache.org/docs/pekko/current/general/configuration-reference.html)
for the available keys.

```yaml
spring:
  actor:
    pekko:
      loglevel: INFO
      coordinated-shutdown:
        phases:
          cluster-leave:
            timeout: 10s
```

!!! note "Raw keys win"
    When a raw key and a typed key set the same Pekko key to different values, the raw key wins and
    the starter logs a warning that names both, for example
    `spring.actor.pekko.name=raw overrides spring.actor.name=typed`. Prefer the typed key.

## Metrics agent environment variables (`ACTOR_METRICS_*`)

!!! warning "Not Spring keys"
    These are environment variables, read by the optional metrics Java agent and by the metrics registry
    builder with `System.getenv` (falling back to a JVM system property of the same name). They are
    not Spring configuration keys: setting them in `application.yml` or `application.properties`
    has no effect, and they do not appear in the Spring configuration metadata.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `ACTOR_METRICS_ENABLED` | `true` | Read by the agent at JVM startup: `false` skips all instrumentation. Also read by the metrics registry builder to set the enabled flag of the metrics configuration. |
| `ACTOR_METRICS_INSTRUMENT_<MODULE>` | `true` | Read by the agent: `false` skips instrumentation for one module. `<MODULE>` is the module id in upper case with `-` replaced by `_`: `ACTOR_LIFECYCLE`, `MESSAGE_PROCESSING`, `MAILBOX`, `SYSTEM`, `SCHEDULER`, `STASH`. |
| `ACTOR_METRICS_TAG_<NAME>` | none | Adds a global tag to every agent metric. The tag name is `<NAME>` in lower case with `_` replaced by `.`; for example `ACTOR_METRICS_TAG_APPLICATION=my-app` adds the tag `application=my-app`. |
| `ACTOR_METRICS_SAMPLING_RATE` | `1.0` | Sampling rate between `0.0` and `1.0`. |

```bash
ACTOR_METRICS_TAG_APPLICATION=my-app \
ACTOR_METRICS_INSTRUMENT_MAILBOX=false \
java -javaagent:actor-metrics-{version}-agent.jar -jar app.jar
```

## Related

- [Running in Production](production.md): shutdown and health settings in context
- [Monitoring](monitoring.md): what the metrics keys turn on
- [Cluster Formation](../cluster/cluster-formation.md), [Split Brain and Leases](../cluster/split-brain-and-leases.md)
- [Dispatchers](../core/dispatchers.md)

<!-- Source: https://seonwkim.github.io/actor-spring-boot-starter/guides/testing/ -->

# Testing

The `actor-test` module has three tools for tests:

- **`@ActorTest`**: a test slice that starts the actor system and your actor beans, and nothing else.
- **`ActorCluster`**: several nodes of your application in one JVM, each on a port it binds itself, for cluster tests.
- **Contract suites**: the tests every `PeerRegistry` and `LeaseStore` must pass, to run against your own store,
  plus in-memory fakes of both.

Add it as a test dependency:

=== "Gradle"

    ```groovy
    testImplementation 'io.github.seonwkim:actor-test:1.0.0'
    ```

=== "Maven"

    ```xml
    <dependency>
        <groupId>io.github.seonwkim</groupId>
        <artifactId>actor-test</artifactId>
        <version>1.0.0</version>
        <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
    ```

`actor-test` has no Pekko types in its API. It brings JUnit 5 and Spring Boot's test support, not the
starter: your application already has that.

## Test actors with `@ActorTest`

`@ActorTest` works like Spring Boot's `@DataJpaTest` or `@WebMvcTest`. It finds your `@SpringBootApplication`,
turns its auto-configuration off and keeps only actor beans from the component scan. You get the
`SpringActorSystem` and every `SpringActor` and `SpringShardedActor` bean, without a web server, a
`DataSource` or your services. Only configuration properties, Jackson and Spring's task executor are
auto-configured, because the actor system uses them when they are there.

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @ActorTest
    class GreeterActorTest {

        @Autowired
        SpringActorSystem actorSystem;

        @Test
        void greets() throws Exception {
            String reply = actorSystem.actor(GreeterActor.class)
                    .withId("greeter")
                    .spawnAndWait()
                    .ask(new GreeterActor.Greet("Ada"))
                    .execute()
                    .toCompletableFuture()
                    .get();

            assertThat(reply).isEqualTo("hello Ada");
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @ActorTest
    class GreeterActorTest {

        @Autowired
        lateinit var actorSystem: SpringActorSystem

        @Test
        fun greets() = runBlocking<Unit> {
            val reply: String = actorSystem.actor<GreeterActor, _>()
                .withId("greeter")
                .awaitSpawn()
                .awaitAsk(GreeterActor.Greet("Ada"))

            assertThat(reply).isEqualTo("hello Ada")
        }
    }
    ```

In Kotlin, `runBlocking` (from `kotlinx-coroutines-core`, which `actor-kotlin` brings) runs the `suspend` calls
in the test. Name actors to start only those, and add properties:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    @ActorTest(actors = GreeterActor.class, properties = "spring.actor.name=greeter-test")
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    @ActorTest(actors = [GreeterActor::class], properties = ["spring.actor.name=greeter-test"])
    ```

An actor that needs another bean gets it with `@Import(MyService.class)` or `@MockitoBean`. `includeFilters`,
`excludeFilters` and `excludeAutoConfiguration` work as on Spring Boot's own slices.

The actor system is the one your application's auto-configuration starts: the slice imports the same
actor auto-configurations, so `spring.actor.*` properties from `application.yml` apply.

## Cluster tests with `ActorCluster`

`ActorCluster` starts several Spring contexts of your application in one JVM. Each node binds port 0, so
the operating system gives it a free port as it binds and no other test or process can take that port in
between. Node 1 joins itself (`spring.actor.cluster.join-self`) and forms the cluster at once; the others
join it at the address it bound. `start()` returns when every node sees every node up. With Pekko
Management on the classpath, each node's management server binds port 0 too.

With JUnit 5, register `ActorClusterExtension`. On an instance field it starts a cluster for each test; on a
static field (in Kotlin, a `@JvmField` in a `companion object`), one for the whole class.

=== "Java"

    ```java
    class ShardedCounterClusterTest {

        @RegisterExtension
        final ActorClusterExtension cluster = new ActorClusterExtension(
                ActorCluster.builder(MyApplication.class)
                        .nodes(3)
                        .roles(1, "frontend")
                        .properties("app.feature.enabled=true"));

        @Test
        void anEntityKeepsItsStateWhenANodeLeaves() {
            SpringActorSystem first = cluster.node(1).getBean(SpringActorSystem.class);
            // ... message a sharded entity from node 1

            cluster.cluster().stop(2);
            cluster.cluster().awaitMembersUp(2);
            // ... the entity answers from another node
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    class ShardedCounterClusterTest {

        @JvmField
        @RegisterExtension
        val cluster = ActorClusterExtension(
            ActorCluster.builder(MyApplication::class.java)
                .nodes(3)
                .roles(1, "frontend")
                .properties("app.feature.enabled=true"))

        @Test
        fun anEntityKeepsItsStateWhenANodeLeaves() {
            val first = cluster.node(1).getBean(SpringActorSystem::class.java)
            // ... message a sharded entity from node 1

            cluster.cluster().stop(2)
            cluster.cluster().awaitMembersUp(2)
            // ... the entity answers from another node
        }
    }
    ```

Without JUnit, use it directly; it is `AutoCloseable`:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    try (ActorCluster cluster = ActorCluster.builder(MyApplication.class).nodes(3).start()) {
        // ...
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    ActorCluster.builder(MyApplication::class.java).nodes(3).start().use { cluster ->
        // ...
    }
    ```

| Builder method | What it sets |
|---|---|
| `nodes(int)` | Number of nodes, 3 by default |
| `systemName(String)` | The actor system name of every node |
| `properties(String...)` | `key=value` properties for every node |
| `nodeProperties(int, String...)` | Properties for one node, numbered from 1 |
| `roles(int, String...)` | Cluster roles of one node |
| `timeout(Duration)` | How long to wait for members to be up, 30 seconds by default |
| `classLoader(int, ClassLoader)` | The class loader one node, numbered from 1, loads your classes through. Use it to run two versions of a class side by side |

The properties are passed as command-line arguments, so they override your `application.yml`. The
cluster tracks membership through the starter's cluster events: `upMembers(node)` is the number of members a
node sees up, and `awaitMembersUp(count)` waits until every running node sees that many.

### Two versions of a message in one cluster

To check that a message change survives a rolling update, run one node on the next version of the message
class. Compile the new version into its own folder (for example with `javax.tools.JavaCompiler` in the
test), and give that node a class loader that loads the class from there and every other class from your
application:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    ClassLoader v2 = new ClassLoader(getClass().getClassLoader()) {
        @Override
        protected Class<?> loadClass(String name, boolean resolve) throws ClassNotFoundException {
            if (!name.equals(SayHello.class.getName())) {
                return super.loadClass(name, resolve);
            }
            synchronized (getClassLoadingLock(name)) {
                Class<?> loaded = findLoadedClass(name);
                if (loaded == null) {
                    byte[] bytes = readClassFile(v2Classes, name); // your helper: the .class file's bytes
                    loaded = defineClass(name, bytes, 0, bytes.length);
                }
                return loaded;
            }
        }
    };

    try (ActorCluster cluster = ActorCluster.builder(MyApplication.class)
            .nodes(2)
            .classLoader(2, v2)
            .start()) {
        // Node 1 sends the old SayHello to an entity on node 2, and node 2 sends the new one
        // (created through v2.loadClass(...)) to an entity on node 1.
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    val v2 = object : ClassLoader(javaClass.classLoader) {
        override fun loadClass(name: String, resolve: Boolean): Class<*> {
            if (name != SayHello::class.java.name) {
                return super.loadClass(name, resolve)
            }
            synchronized(getClassLoadingLock(name)) {
                return findLoadedClass(name) ?: readClassFile(v2Classes, name) // your helper: the .class file's bytes
                    .let { bytes -> defineClass(name, bytes, 0, bytes.size) }
            }
        }
    }

    ActorCluster.builder(MyApplication::class.java)
        .nodes(2)
        .classLoader(2, v2)
        .start()
        .use { cluster ->
            // Node 1 sends the old SayHello to an entity on node 2, and node 2 sends the new one
            // (created through v2.loadClass(...)) to an entity on node 1.
        }
    ```

Put the entities on a given node with a role (`roles(1, "v1")` and `role()` on the sharded actor), so each
message really crosses between the versions. The starter's own build runs this test
(`MixedVersionMessageTest` in `actor-cluster`).

## Contract suites for your own store

A `PeerRegistry` or `LeaseStore` of your own ([Cluster Formation](cluster/cluster-formation.md#your-own-store),
[Split Brain and Leases](cluster/split-brain-and-leases.md#your-own-store)) must behave like the built-in ones: for
example, of twenty nodes that try to take a lease at once, exactly one wins. `actor-test` publishes the
tests the built-in JDBC and Redis stores pass. Extend the suite and return your store:

=== "Java"

    ```java
    class MyLeaseStoreContractTest extends LeaseStoreContract {

        private final MyLeaseStore store = new MyLeaseStore(testDatabase());

        @Override
        protected LeaseStore store() {
            return store;
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    class MyLeaseStoreContractTest : LeaseStoreContract() {

        private val store = MyLeaseStore(testDatabase())

        override fun store(): LeaseStore = store
    }
    ```

=== "Java"

    ```java
    class MyPeerRegistryContractTest extends PeerRegistryContract {

        @Override
        protected PeerRegistry registry() {
            return new MyPeerRegistry(testDatabase());
        }
    }
    ```

=== "Kotlin"

    ```kotlin
    class MyPeerRegistryContractTest : PeerRegistryContract() {

        override fun registry(): PeerRegistry = MyPeerRegistry(testDatabase())
    }
    ```

Each test uses its own lease or service name, so one store may serve every test. Some tests wait for a
ttl of one to two seconds to pass, because stores may keep time in whole seconds.

`InMemoryPeerRegistry` and `InMemoryLeaseStore` pass the same suites. Declare one as a bean to run cluster
tests with `discovery.method: custom` or `lease.store: custom` without a database; nodes in one JVM can
share one instance.

## Related

- [Kotlin](kotlin.md): the `suspend` helpers used in the Kotlin tests
- [Cluster Formation](cluster/cluster-formation.md) and [Split Brain and Leases](cluster/split-brain-and-leases.md): the stores the contract suites cover
- [Sharded Actors](cluster/sharded-actors.md)

<!-- Source: https://seonwkim.github.io/actor-spring-boot-starter/guides/kotlin/ -->

# Kotlin

The `actor-kotlin` module adds a thin Kotlin layer over the Java API: a `behavior { }` DSL for actor
behaviors, `suspend` functions instead of `CompletionStage`, reified type parameters instead of `Class`
arguments, and `kotlin.time.Duration` timeouts. Each function calls the Java API, so everything in the other guides applies unchanged.

## Installation

Add `actor-kotlin` next to the starter. It brings `kotlinx-coroutines-core`; Spring Boot manages its
version.

```kotlin
dependencies {
    implementation("io.github.seonwkim:actor-spring-boot-starter:1.0.0")
    implementation("io.github.seonwkim:actor-kotlin:1.0.0")
}
```

The module is compiled with Kotlin 1.9.25, the version Spring Boot 3.5 manages, so applications on that
version or later can use it.

### Null safety

`actor-api` declares its nullability: values are non-null unless marked `@Nullable` (for example
`AskCommand.getReplyTo()`). Kotlin turns those annotations into Kotlin types with the
`-Xjsr305=strict` compiler flag, which projects generated by start.spring.io already set:

```kotlin
kotlin {
    compilerOptions {
        freeCompilerArgs.addAll("-Xjsr305=strict")
    }
}
```

Without the flag, Kotlin only warns, and the API's types are platform types (`String!`).

## Defining an actor

`behavior<Command>(actorContext) { ... }` builds the behavior with `SpringActorBehavior.builder`.
Commands are often a sealed interface:

```kotlin
@Component
class HelloActor : SpringActor<HelloActor.Command> {
    sealed interface Command

    class SayHello : AskCommand<String>(), Command

    data class LogVisit(val name: String) : Command

    override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        behavior<Command>(actorContext) {
            onMessage<SayHello> { msg ->
                msg.reply("Hello from actor ${actorContext.actorId()}")
                same()
            }
            onMessage<LogVisit> { msg ->
                log.info("{} visited", msg.name)   // the behavior context is `this`
                same()
            }
        }
}
```

Inside the block:

| DSL | Java builder |
|---|---|
| `onMessage<M> { msg -> next }` | `.onMessage(M.class, (ctx, msg) -> next)` |
| `onSignal<PostStop> { signal -> next }` | `.onSignal(PostStop.class, (ctx, signal) -> next)` |
| `withSupervisionStrategy(strategy)` | `.withSupervisionStrategy(strategy)` |
| `withMdc { msg -> mapOf(...) }` | `.withMdc(msg -> Map.of(...))` |
| `same()`, `stopped()`, `unhandled()` | `SpringActorBehavior.same()`, `.stopped()`, `.unhandled()` |

A handler runs with the behavior context as `this`, so `self`, `log`, `pipeToSelf(...)`, `watch(...)` and
the timers need no `ctx.` prefix. It returns the next behavior: `same()`, `stopped()`, `unhandled()`, or
another `behavior { }` to switch behaviors.

### State

To keep state in an object, pass a `state` factory ([`withState`](core/behaviors.md#state-with-withstate)).
It runs when the actor starts and again on each restart, and the handlers then run with the state object as
`this`:

```kotlin
override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
    behavior<Command, Counter>(actorContext, state = { ctx -> Counter(ctx) }) {
        onMessage<Add> { msg -> onAdd(msg) }
        onMessage<Get> { msg -> onGet(msg) }
    }
```

`behavior<Command, _>` works too: Kotlin infers the state type from the factory.

`actorBehavior<Command>(actorContext)` returns the Java builder itself, for code that prefers the chained
`.onMessage(Type::class.java) { ctx, msg -> ... }.build()` style.

## Spawning and finding actors

The reified helpers take the actor type as a type argument. Kotlin can't infer the command type from
the actor type by itself, so pass `_` for it:

```kotlin
// actorSystem.actor(HelloActor::class.java)
val builder = actorSystem.actor<HelloActor, _>()

// Suspends until the actor runs
val hello: SpringActorHandle<HelloActor.Command> =
    actorSystem.actor<HelloActor, _>().withId("hello").withTimeout(5.seconds).awaitSpawn()

val running = actorSystem.awaitGetOrSpawn<HelloActor, _>("hello") // spawn when none runs
val maybe = actorSystem.awaitGet<HelloActor, _>("hello")          // null when none runs
val exists = actorSystem.awaitExists<HelloActor, _>("hello")

// Sharded actors (cluster mode)
val counter = actorSystem.sharded<CounterActor, _>().withId("counter-1").get()
```

| Kotlin | Java API it calls |
|---|---|
| `actor<A, _>()` | `actor(A.class)` |
| `sharded<A, _>()` | `sharded(A.class)` |
| `awaitGetOrSpawn<A, _>(id)`, `awaitGet<A, _>(id)`, `awaitExists<A, _>(id)` | `getOrSpawn`, `find` (as a nullable), `exists` with `A.class` |
| `builder.awaitSpawn()`, `builder.awaitGetOrSpawn()` | `spawn()`, `getOrSpawn()` on the spawn builder |
| `behavior<C>(actorContext) { }`, `behavior<C, S>(actorContext, state = { ctx -> S(ctx) }) { }` | `SpringActorBehavior.builder(C.class, actorContext)`, then `withState`, the handlers and `build()` |
| `actorBehavior<C>(actorContext)` | `SpringActorBehavior.builder(C.class, actorContext)` |
| `handle.child<A, _>()`, `handle.child<A, _>(id)` | `child(A.class)`, `child(A.class, id)` |
| `awaitSpawn()`, `awaitGetOrSpawn()`, `awaitExists()` on a child builder; `awaitGet()`, `awaitExists()` on a child reference | `spawn()`, `getOrSpawn()`, `get()`, `exists()` |
| `withTimeout(5.seconds)`, `withLimit(10, 1.minutes)`, `startSingleTimer(key, msg, 30.seconds)`, `startTimerAtFixedRate(key, msg, 10.seconds)` | the same methods with a `java.time.Duration` |
| `unwrap<X>()` on the actor system, a ref or a behavior context | `unwrap(X.class)` |

## Child actors

`handle.child<A, _>()` is the child builder and `handle.child<A, _>(id)` the lookup reference of
[Child actors](core/actors.md#child-actors). Outside the parent, the `await*` functions suspend until the
operation completes. A child lookup returns `null` when the child doesn't run:

```kotlin
// In a suspend function, with the parent's handle
val worker = dispatcher.child<WorkerActor, _>()
    .withId("worker-1")
    .withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart().withLimit(10, 1.minutes))
    .withTimeout(5.seconds)
    .awaitGetOrSpawn()

val found: SpringActorHandle<WorkerActor.Command>? = dispatcher.child<WorkerActor, _>("worker-1").awaitGet()
val running: Boolean = dispatcher.child<WorkerActor, _>("worker-1").awaitExists()
```

Inside the parent's own handlers, don't wait: pass `spawn()` or `getOrSpawn()` to `pipeToSelf`, as in
[Spawning children from inside the parent](core/actors.md#spawning-children-from-inside-the-parent).

## Durations

These methods also take a `kotlin.time.Duration`: `withTimeout` on the spawn, sharded, child and ask
builders and on the child reference, `SupervisionStrategy.restart().withLimit`, and the timers on the
behavior context:

```kotlin
ctx.startSingleTimer("idle", IdleTimeout, 30.minutes)
ctx.startTimerAtFixedRate("flush", Flush, 10.seconds)
```

## Asking

`awaitAsk` sends an `AskCommand` and suspends until the reply arrives. Without a timeout, the handle's
default timeout (3 seconds) applies.

```kotlin
val greeting: String = hello.awaitAsk(HelloActor.SayHello(), timeout = 2.seconds)
```

When no reply arrives in time, `awaitAsk` throws `java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException`. For a fallback
value instead, use the ask builder and finish it with `await()`:

```kotlin
val greeting = hello.ask(HelloActor.SayHello())
    .withTimeout(2.seconds)
    .onTimeout { "no answer" }
    .await()
```

`awaitAsk` works the same on a sharded actor handle. Cancelling the coroutine stops the wait; the
command has already been sent.

## In a WebFlux controller

With `kotlinx-coroutines-reactor` and `kotlin-reflect` on the classpath, WebFlux runs `suspend` handler functions:

```kotlin
@RestController
class HelloController(private val actorSystem: SpringActorSystem) {
    @GetMapping("/hello")
    suspend fun hello(): String =
        actorSystem.awaitGetOrSpawn<HelloActor, _>("hello-actor")
            .awaitAsk(HelloActor.SayHello(), timeout = 3.seconds)
}
```

The full application is in
[example/kotlin](https://github.com/seonWKim/actor-spring-boot-starter/tree/main/example/kotlin): the
[simple example](../examples/simple.md), written in Kotlin. The [Kotlin example](../examples/kotlin.md) page
walks through it.

## Related

- [Actors](core/actors.md) and [Messaging](core/messaging.md): the Java API these functions call
- [Testing](testing.md): `@ActorTest` with `runBlocking`
